Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verse 1–2:

(p-210) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Hajj (the Pilgrimage, i.e. exegesis of the chapter)

This surah is Meccan except for three verses, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These two adversaries dispute﴾ [al-Hajj: 19] up to the completion of three verses. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are four verses, up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the punishment of the Burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 22]. Al-Dahhak said: it is Medinan. Qatadah said: Surat al-Hajj is Medinan except for four verses, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya: 25], up to His saying: ﴿the punishment of a barren day﴾ [al-Hajj: 55]. These are Meccan. Al-Naqqash counted what was revealed at Medina as ten verses. The majority said: the surah is mixed, some of it Meccan and some of it Medinan. This is the most correct view, and Allah knows best, because the verses require that. It is narrated from Anas ibn Malik that he said: «The beginning of the surah was revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during a journey, so he called out with it and the people gathered to him. He said: Do you know what day this is? They were bewildered. He said: It is the day when Allah says: O Adam, bring forth the company of the Fire. He will bring forth from every thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine. He said: The people were distressed, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Rejoice, for among you is one man, and from Gog and Magog there are a thousand men..." » — the hadith.

(p-211) His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing. On the day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from that which she nursed, and every pregnant one will lay down her burden, and you will see people as intoxicated, but they are not intoxicated; rather, the punishment of Allah is severe.﴾

The beginning of the verse is a warning to all the world. Then the report emphasised and confirmed it with the matter of the convulsion of the Resurrection, which is one of its signs. He called it "a thing" because its occurrence is certain, and so it is fitting to call it a thing though it is non-existent, since certainty of it makes it like existing things. As for "in its outcome" (al-ma'al), i.e. it, when it occurs, is a tremendous thing, it is as if he did not apply the name now; rather the meaning is: if it is, then at that time it is a tremendous thing.

And "al-zalzala" (the convulsion) is a great shaking. That is with the blast of terror and with the blast of swooning, as the hadith of Abu Hurayrah includes, of three blasts. From the word "zalzala" is the saying of the poet:

؎ The ignorant, misguided one knows that time has in it calamity and convulsion.

It is possible that "al-zalzala" in the verse is an expression for the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿They were touched by misfortune and adversity and were shaken﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214], and as he, peace be upon him, said: «O Allah, defeat them and shake them». (p-212) The majority hold that the convulsion of the Hour is like the one known in this world, except that it is in extreme severity.

The exegetes differed concerning the mentioned "convulsion": is it in this world upon the people over whom the Resurrection will rise, or is it on the Day of Resurrection upon the whole world? The majority said: it is in this world, and the pronoun in "you see it" refers to the convulsion. What strengthened their view is that suckling and pregnancy are in this world. A group said: the "convulsion" is on the Day of Resurrection, and they argued with the hadith of Anas mentioned just above, since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited the verse and then said: «It is the day on which He says to Adam: Bring forth the company of the Fire».

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This hadith is no proof, because it is possible that the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse which includes the beginning of the matter of the Hour, then intended, in his reminding and warning, a particular section of the events of the Day of Resurrection and specified its mention; this is of eloquence. According to this group the pronoun refers to the Hour, i.e. the day on which they see its beginning in this world, so by this interpretation it is valid for them that the existence of suckling and pregnancy on the Day of Resurrection is not required of them. If they refer it to the convulsion, their view is corrupted by what it entails for them. Moreover, al-Naqqash mentioned that what is meant by "every pregnant one" is the woman who died while her child was in her womb.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak.

And "al-dhuhul" (distraction): heedlessness of a thing by the occurrence of what occupies one from it, such as worry, pain or something else. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: she leaves her child because of the distress that has descended upon her. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "tudhhilu" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha' and a fatha on "kulla", and he attached the ha' to "murdi'a" because he intended those doing that on that day, so he treated it as the verb. As for when you report about a woman that she has a child she is nursing, (p-213) you say "murdi'" like "hamil". 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: this ha' in "murdi'a" refutes the Kufans' view that the ha' is not present in what does not specifically pertain to men. Al-Tabari related that some Kufan grammarians said: the child's mother is "murdi'a", and the hired nurse for him is "murdi'".

And "al-haml" with a fatha on the ha': what is in a belly or on the top of a tree. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you see people as intoxicated﴾ is a likening of them; i.e. from grief. Then He negated from them the true intoxication which is from wine, as al-Hasan and others said.

The majority of reciters read "sukara" with a damma on the sin and the alif retained, and likewise in the second place. This is the pattern: once Sibawayh made it a plural, and once a collective noun. Abu Hurayrah read it with a fatha on the sin in both places, and this too may occur in these plurals. Abu al-Fath said: it is a broken plural. Abu Hatim said: it is the dialect of Tamim. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sakra" in both places; it was narrated by 'Imran ibn Husayn and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri from the Prophet ﷺ, and it is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Hudhayfah, and the companions of 'Abd Allah. Sibawayh said: some people say "sakra", making it like "marda", because they are two states that come upon a person; then they made "rawba" like "sakra", and they are those heavy with sleep from drinking whey. Abu 'Ali said: it is possible that "sakra" is the plural of "sukr" like "zamani" and "zaman". Sibawayh has related: "rajul sakir" meaning "sakran" (drunk), so "sakra" then comes for the feminine of the plural, as the sign in "ta'ifa" is for the feminine of the collective. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read: "wa tara al-nasa sakra wa ma hum bi-sukara" with a damma and the alif. Al-Mahdawi related from al-Hasan that he read: "wa tara al-nasa sukara wa ma hum bi-sakra". (p-214) Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and Abu Zar'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir read in both places "sukra" with a damma on the sin. Abu al-Fath said: it is a singular noun like "al-bushra", and Abu 'Ali gave me this ruling when I asked him about it. Abu Zar'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir, Abu Hurayrah, and Abu Nahik read "wa tura" with a damma on the ta' and "al-nasa" in the accusative, and he said: it is only according to its meaning. This reading has also been transmitted as "wa turá al-nasu" with a damma on the ta' and the sin; i.e., you see the multitude of people.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 22, verses 3–5**

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Among mankind is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge, and follows every rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿It has been decreed for him that whoever takes him as a friend, he will lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We cause to remain in the wombs whatever We will for an appointed term. Then We bring you out as infants, then that you may reach your maturity. And among you is one who is taken in death, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows after knowledge nothing.﴾

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Among mankind﴾ – the verse. Ibn Jurayj said: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and Ubayy ibn Khalaf. It was also said: concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. Then it encompasses, beyond them, everyone who is characterised by this attribute.

"Al-mujadala" (disputation) means argumentation (al-muhajja), and its root is taken from "al-jadal," which means twisting. The meaning of "yujadilu" is that he disputes concerning Allah's power and His attributes. The occasion of the verse was the speech of those who claimed that Allah, blessed and exalted, does not resurrect the dead and does not restore bodies from graves.

"Al-shaytan" here is their misleader from among the jinn. It is possible that the shaytan is from among mankind, and "al-inhaa" (condemnation) is directed at those who follow him. "Al-marid" (rebellious) is one who is stripped of good and turned toward evil. From it comes "al-amrad" (the beardless youth), and "shajara mardaa" (a tree stripped bare), meaning devoid of leaves; and "sarh mumarrad" (a smooth palace), meaning made smooth of glass; and "sakhra mardaa," meaning a smooth rock.

The pronoun in "ʿalayhi" refers to the shaytan, as Qatada said, and it is possible that it refers to the disputer. "Annahu" is in the position of the nominative as the unnamed agent (in the passive construction). The second "annahu" is a conjunction linked to the first, emphasising it similarly. It was also said: the second is merely a repetition for emphasis. This is objected to on the ground that a thing is not emphasised until it is complete, and the completion of the first "annahu" is only with its clause, which is in His saying "al-Saʿir." Likewise, it is not conjoined to it. According to Sibawayh, in such a case it is a substitute (badal). It was also said that the second "annahu" is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimation being: "then his affair is that he misleads him." Abu ʿAli estimated it as: "then it is for him to mislead him."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What appears to me is that the pronoun in the first "annahu" refers to the shaytan, and in the second to "man" (whoever), who is the one who takes him as a friend. His saying "wa-yahdihi" means: he directs him to the path of that, and it is not in the sense of guidance in the absolute sense. Abu ʿAmr recited "innahu man tawallahu fa-innahu yudilluhu" with the kasra in both places.

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection﴾ – the verse. This is an argument addressed to the world through the first beginning. Allah, may He be exalted, has set forth in this verse two examples which, if the observer considers them, permit in reason the resurrection from graves; then the report of the Law came with the obligation of that and its occurrence. "Al-rayb" is doubt. His saying "in kuntum" is a conditional clause whose implication is affirmation/reproach. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "al-baʿtha" with a fatha on the ʿayn. It is a dialect of "al-baʿth" according to the Basrans, and according to the Kufans it is a lightened form of "baʿatha."

His saying: ﴿We created you from dust﴾ means Adam. Then the verb is applied to them, inasmuch as they are his descendants. His saying: ﴿then from a drop of semen﴾ means the seed that comes from humans. "Al-nutfa" applies to a little water and to a lot of it. Al-Naqqash said: what is meant is the seed of Adam. His saying: ﴿then from a clinging clot﴾ means from blood, to which the seed returns in the womb, or what accompanies the seed. "Al-ʿalaq" is fresh (congealed) blood. It was also said: "al-ʿalaq" is that which is intensely red, and blood is named after that. His saying: "then from a lump of flesh" means a piece of flesh the size of what can be chewed. His saying: "formed" (mukhallaqa) means with its structure completed, and "unformed" (ghayr mukhallaqa) means not completed, that is, the one which falls. This was said by Mujahid, Qatada, al-Shaʿbi, and Abu al-ʿAliya. The word is thus a form of intensification from "khalaqa." Since the human being has distinct members, each of which is specialised in a fine form, the whole intensifies the verb, because there are many forms in it. Ibn Abi ʿAbla recited "mukhallaqatan" with the accusative and "ghayra" with the accusative in the rāʾ.

(p-216) Connected to this place in jurisprudence is that the scholars differed concerning the umm walad (a slave woman who bore her master a child) if she miscarries a piece of flesh that has not taken shape. Is she an umm walad by that? Malik, al-Awzaʿi, and others said: she is an umm walad by the lump of flesh if it is known that it is the lump of the child. Al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifa said: not until a creation appears in it, even if it is a single limb.

His saying: ﴿that We may make clear to you﴾. One group said: its meaning is: that We may make clear to you the matter of resurrection. Thus it is a parenthetical clause between the two statements. This group recited "nuqirru" with the nominative, the meaning being "and We cause to remain," and this is the reading of the majority. Another group said: "li-nubayyina lakum" means: the lump is unformed and women cast it out; thus We make clear to people that the changes in the womb are like this. This group recited "wa-nuqirra" with the accusative, and likewise recited "nukhrijakum" with the accusative. This is the transmission of al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim. Abu ʿAmr al-Dani related that the transmission of al-Mufaddal is with the yāʾ in "yuqirru" and "yukhrijukum," and the nominative is common on this interpretation, while the accusative is not permitted on the first interpretation. Ibn Wathhab recited "ma nashaʾu" with a kasra on the nun. "Al-ajal al-musamma" (the appointed term) differs according to each foetus: there is one that is miscarried, and there is one whose matter is completed and comes out alive.

People differed concerning "al-ashadd" (full maturity): it is said to be eighteen, to thirty, to thirty-two, to thirty-six, to forty, to forty-five. The word is used in a shared sense (ishtirak), so the maturity of a human in general is other than the maturity of an orphan, which is puberty (al-ihtilam). The word "al-ashadd" in the verse may bear both meanings. The return to the most abject age (ardhal al-ʿumr) is the arrival of a person at senility and the disruption of his strength, so that he cannot perform the acts of worship, and the disruption of his intellect, so that he cannot uphold what his beliefs require of him. This always accompanies old age, though it may occur at a young age according to the individual, when he is afflicted by a chronic illness. It has been reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that the most abject age is seventy-five years. This is open to question, and even if it is authentically from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, it is only sound if he meant: for most people, since we see many who are eighty years old who are not in the most abject age. The majority recited "al-ʿumur" (with the vowel fully pronounced), while Nafiʿ recited "al-ʿumur" with the mīm lightened, and his transmission differed on this.

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿so that he knows﴾, meaning: so that he forgets his acquaintances and the knowledge he had, so that he knows nothing of that. This single example suffices for whoever considers it, to establish that the One capable of these changes, and skilled in them, is capable of restoring those bodies that He brought into being through these changes to their original state.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 22, verses 3–5**

And We cause to remain in the wombs whatever We will for an appointed term. Then We bring you out as infants, then that you may reach your maturity. And among you is one who is taken in death, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows after knowledge nothing.﴾

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Among mankind﴾ – the verse. Ibn Jurayj said: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and Ubayy ibn Khalaf. It was also said: concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. Then it encompasses, beyond them, everyone who is characterised by this attribute.

"Al-mujadala" (disputation) means argumentation (al-muhajja), and its root is taken from "al-jadal," which means twisting. The meaning of "yujadilu" is that he disputes concerning Allah's power and His attributes. The occasion of the verse was the speech of those who claimed that Allah, blessed and exalted, does not resurrect the dead and does not restore bodies from graves.

"Al-shaytan" here is their misleader from among the jinn. It is possible that the shaytan is from among mankind, and "al-inhaa" (condemnation) is directed at those who follow him. "Al-marid" (rebellious) is one who is stripped of good and turned toward evil. From it comes "al-amrad" (the beardless youth), and "shajara mardaa" (a tree stripped bare), meaning devoid of leaves; and "sarh mumarrad" (a smooth palace), meaning made smooth of glass; and "sakhra mardaa," meaning a smooth rock.

It was also said: the second is merely a repetition for emphasis. This is objected to on the ground that a thing is not emphasised until it is complete, and the completion of the first "annahu" is only with its clause, which is in His saying "al-Saʿir." Likewise, it is not conjoined to it. According to Sibawayh, in such a case it is a substitute (badal). Abu ʿAli estimated it as: "then it is for him to mislead him."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verses 11–13:

The words of the Most High:

﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge. If good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.﴾ ﴿He calls upon, besides Allah, that which can neither harm him nor benefit him. That is the far-off error.﴾ ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. Evil is the protector, and evil is the companion.﴾

These verses were revealed concerning the Bedouins (a'rab) and people who had no firm certainty (yaqin). One of them would embrace Islam, and then he would experience some favourable outcomes: an increase in wealth, a male child whom Allah grants him, and other such things. He would say, "This is a good religion," and he would hold fast to it for these benefits. But if the matter went contrary to this, he would consider it an ill omen and apostatise, as the 'Urayniyyun and others did. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and others.

As for His saying, "on an edge" (ʿalā ḥarf), its meaning is: on a deviation from the pure belief, or on the brink of it, prepared to fall away. "Fitna" means testing. His saying, ﴿he turns back on his face﴾, is a metaphor for one who turns away from affairs. As for "he has lost this world and the Hereafter": as for this world, it is by the decrees that have passed over him; as for the Hereafter, it is by his apostasy and the evil of his belief. Mujahid, Hamza and al-A'raj read "khāsira al-dunyā wal-ākhirah" in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

As for His saying, ﴿that which can neither harm him nor benefit him﴾, it refers to idols. The meaning of "yad'u" here is "worships," and it also means "calls upon" in his afflictions. People differed concerning His saying, blessed and exalted is He, ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾. A group among the Kufans said: the lam is placed before its proper position, and the intended sense is: "He calls upon one who harms him." This interpretation is supported by the fact that 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read: "yad'u man ḍarrahu." Al-Akhfash said: "yad'u" here means "yaqūlu" (says), "min" is a subject (mubtada'), "ḍurruhu" is a subject, "aqrabu" is its predicate, and the clause is a relative clause (ṣila); the predicate of "min" is omitted, and the sense is: he says to one whose harm is nearer than his benefit, "A god," and something similar to this is the saying of 'Antara:

"They call 'Antar, and the spears as if they..."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is open to question; consider how it corrupts the meaning, for the unbeliever never believed that the harm of the idols was nearer than their benefit. Abu 'Ali's justification here is evasive, and moreover it does not resemble the line of poetry he cited. It was also said: the meaning of "yad'u" here is "yusammī" (names), and this is like the previous view, except that the omitted object at the end is a direct object, its implied sense being: "a god." Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible for "yad'u" to be in the position of a circumstantial state, and there is a omitted pronoun in it, and the sense is: "That is the far-off error," meaning: "yad'ūhu" (calling upon it), so one stops at this point. Abu 'Ali said: it is also good for "dhālika" to mean "alladhī" (who), that is: "the one who is the far-off error calls upon," so that "dhālika" is a relative construction joined to His saying ﴿is the far-off error﴾, and "yad'u" governs the word "dhālika."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Al-'Ashir" means the close companion who associates with one in affairs. Al-Tabari held that what is meant by "al-mawla" and "al-'ashir" is the idol whose harm is nearer than its benefit, and this is the view of Mujahid. And Allah knows best.

(p-222) When God, blessed and exalted, mentioned those who worship Him on an edge (ʿalā ḥarf), declared their opinion foolish, and threatened them with the loss of the Hereafter, He followed this with mention of their opponents among the people of faith, and mentioned what He had promised them: that He would admit them into the Garden. Then the verse turned to rebuking those first ones and to their leaving the matter to their own opinion and to what would bring them distress rather than ease. It is as if it says: these who worship on an edge, unease has accompanied them, and they assumed that God, exalted, would not give victory to Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, and his followers. We have only commanded them to be patient and to await Our promise. As for the fāʾ and the wāw, when one of them enters upon the imperative, Sibawayh related that they treat it as if it were part of the word, so the sukūn of the lām is a lightening, and it is more eloquent than vocalizing it. As for "thumma," it is an independent word, so the proper course is to vocalize the lām after it.

(p-224) The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Some grammarians regarded the mīm of "thumma" as equivalent to the wāw and the fāʾ.

His saying, exalted is He, "mā yaghīẓu" (what enrages), may be that "mā" means "alladhī" (that which), and in "yaghīẓu" there is a pronoun referring back to it. It may also be that it is a verbal particle (maṣdariyya), so there is no pronoun referring back to it. And "al-kayd" (scheming) is his stretching of the rope.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The clearest of the aspects of this verse is that it be a parable (mathal), with "al-naṣr" meaning the well-known victory, "al-qaṭʿ" meaning strangulation, and "al-samāʾ" meaning elevation in the air by means of a ceiling, a tree or the like. So consider it.

As for His saying, exalted is He: "And thus We have sent it down as clear signs," up to "over everything He is witness," the meaning is: just as We promised victory and commanded patience, so too We have sent down the Qur'an as a clear sign for whoever reflects and is guided, not so that he may dictate terms with it and hasten the decree. Al-Tabari said: the meaning is: just as I have made clear My proof against the one who denies My power to revive the dead, so too We have sent it down. The pronoun in "anzalnāhu" refers to the Qur'an. These pronouns came in this way even though no mention preceded them, because the thing pointed to is well known, as in His saying, exalted is He: "until it was hidden behind the veil" [Ṣād 38:32], and others.

His saying, exalted is He: "wa-anna Allāh" (and that God) is in the position of the predicate (khabar) of the subject (ibtidāʾ). The estimate is: "and the matter is that God guides whom He wills." God's guidance, blessed and exalted is He, is His creating right guidance and faith in the human soul.

Then God, exalted is He, informed about His action regarding the groups mentioned: they are the believers in Muhammad, upon him ﷺ, and others; the Jews; and the Sabians. They are a people who worship the angels, face the qibla, affirm God's oneness, and recite the Zabur (Psalms), as Qatada said. Then the Christians, and the Magians, who are the worshippers of fire, the sun and the moon. Then the polytheists, who are the worshippers of idols. Qatada said: the religions are six: five belong to Satan and one to the Merciful. The predicate (khabar) of "inna" is His saying, exalted is He: "inna Allāha yafṣilu baynahum" (God will decide between them). Then "inna" entered upon the predicate as an emphasis, and this was made good by the length of the speech; so it and what follows it are the predicate of the first "inna." Al-Zajjaj compared this verse to the saying of the poet:

*"Indeed the caliph, indeed God has clothed him in the garment of a king, by which endings are hoped for."*

Al-Tabari related it.

(p-225) The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This line is not like the verse, because in the line the predicate is in His saying "bihi turjā al-khawātīm" (by which endings are hoped for), and the second "inna" with its clause is an interjection between the two statements. Then the whole speech was completed at His saying, exalted is He, "al-qiyāma" (the Resurrection), and He resumed the predicate about "inna Allāha tabāraka wa-taʿālā ʿalā kulli shayʾin shahīd" (God, blessed and exalted, is witness over everything) and is knowing of it. This statement suits the separation between the groups, and God's separation, exalted is He, between these groups is by admitting the believers to the Garden and the disbelievers to the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verses 18–22:

The words of the Most High:

﴿Do you not see that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the creatures, and many of mankind; and many deserve the punishment. Whoever Allah disgraces, none can honor him. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.﴾

﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads, by which what is in their bellies and their skins will be melted.﴾ ﴿And for them are hooked rods of iron.﴾ ﴿Every time they want to get out of it from distress, they will be returned into it, and [it will be said], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾

"Do you not see" is an alert, from the sight of the heart. This verse informs that all created beings submit and are subservient to Allah the Exalted. The verse mentions everything that people worship, since among created beings there are greater things than those mentioned, such as the seas, the winds and the air. So "whoever is in the heavens" refers to the angels, and "whoever is on the earth" refers to humans who worship. "The sun" was worshipped by Himyar, who were the people of Bilqis. "The moon" was worshipped by Kinanah, as Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said. Tamim worshipped al-Dabaran, Lakhm worshipped Jupiter (al-Mushtari), Tayy worshipped al-Thurayya, Quraysh worshipped al-Shi'ra, Asad worshipped 'Utarid, and Rabi'ah worshipped al-Mirzam. "The mountains and the trees" include fire, idols of stone and wood. "The creatures" include cattle and other animals worshipped, such as the rooster and the like.

"Prostration" (al-sujud) in this verse means submission and compliance with the command. This is like the words of the poet:

"... you see the sand-hills in it prostrating to the hooves."

This is a case where ordinary prostration is impossible. Mujahid said: the prostration of these things is their being nullified. Some said: their prostration is the manifestation of craftsmanship in them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is an error; they confused this verse with the verse of glorification (tasbih). There, it is possible to say that it means the traces of craftsmanship.

The words of Allah, "and many deserve the punishment," may be coordinated with what preceded, meaning: and many deserve the punishment, prostrating unwillingly, that is, out of aversion and against their will, either by submitting when faced with hardships and the like. Mujahid said this, and said: their prostration is by their shadow. It may also be a nominative beginning (mubtada') cut off from what precedes it, as if the clause is set in parallel with the words "and many of mankind," because the meaning is that they are granted mercy through their prostration. This is supported by the words of Allah the Exalted after it: "Whoever Allah disgraces," and so on.

Most readers recited "fa-ma lahu min mukrim" with a kasra on the ra' (ra'). Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it with a fatha on the ra', meaning "from any place," or as a verbal noun (masdar) like madkhal. Most readers recited "wa-l-dawabb" with a doubled ba' (shaddah). Al-Zuhri alone read it with a single ba' (takhfif). This is rare and weak, and it is a lightening contrary to analogy, as they said: zallat and ahassat, and as 'Alqamah said:

"As if their ewer were a gazelle on a height, / Prepared with the threads of linen, veiled."

He meant: bi-sara'ib al-kattan (with the strands of linen). Abu 'Ali cited a similar example:

"Until, when I found nothing but evil, / I became a man of Malik ibn Ja'far."

This is a feature used only in poetry, so this reading is weak.

The words of Allah the Exalted: "These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord," and so on. People differed about what is indicated by "these two" (hadhani). Qays ibn 'Ubada and Hilal ibn Yasaf said: this verse was revealed concerning the duellists on the day of Badr. They were six: Hamzah, 'Ali, and 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, who came out against 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "I am the first to kneel down for the dispute before Allah on the Day of Resurrection." Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) swore to this statement.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It occurs that the verse about them is in the Sahih of al-Bukhari (may Allah have mercy on him).

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: the indication is to the believers and the People of the Book, because a dispute occurred between them. The Jews said, "We are older in religion than you," and similar things, so the verse was revealed. 'Ikrimah said: the dispute is between Paradise and Hell. Mujahid, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, 'Asim, and al-Kalbi said: the indication is to believers and disbelievers in general.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is a view that the verse supports, because the words "and many of mankind" came before, meaning: they are believers who prostrate. Then He said: "and many deserve the punishment," then He indicated these two categories with the words "these two adversaries." The meaning is that faith and its people, and disbelief and its people, are two adversaries, who have been in enmity, dispute and war since the beginning until the Hour arrives. The words "two adversaries" mean two groups, because the word khasm is a verbal noun that is used as an adjective for both the plural and the singular. What shows that He meant the plural is the words "they disputed" (ikhtasamu), which is the reading of most readers. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "ikhtasama" (dual). The words "concerning their Lord" mean: concerning the matter of their Lord, His attributes and His oneness. It may also mean: concerning the pleasure of their Lord, and concerning His essence.

Then He explained the ruling for the two groups. The Blessed and Exalted threatened the disbelievers with the punishment of Hell. "Qutti'at" means: garments were made for them by measure, as a garment is cut out. It is narrated that they are made of brass. It was said: there is no stone hotter than it when it is heated. It is narrated concerning the pouring of the hamim (boiling water) that their heads are struck with the hooked rods so that their brains are exposed, and then the hamim is poured. It was said: rather, the hamim is poured first, which does what is described, and then they are struck with the hooked rods after that. "Al-hamim" is boiling water. "Yusharu" means: it is melted. It was said: it means: it is squeezed. This expression is troubling. It was said: it means: it is cooked. From this is the saying of the poet:

"... the sun melts it, but it does not melt."

As for those who say "it is squeezed," what it resembles is that the hamim descends into the belly, each time it is poured, and scrapes and strips it. Abu Hurayrah narrated something similar from the Prophet (ﷺ): "It strips it, reaches his feet with it, and melts it, then it returns as it was." The majority read "yusharu." A group read "yusahharu" with a fatha on the sad and a shaddah on the ha'. "Al-miq'amah" (with a kasra on the mim) is a rod of iron with which the one being struck is beaten.

The words of Allah the Exalted "they wish" (aradu): it is narrated concerning this that when the flame of the fire rises, it lifts them up until they reach the gates of the fire, and then they wish to exit, and they are struck with the hooked rods, and the angels of punishment (al-zabaniyah) push them back. The "min" in His words "minha" (from it) indicates the starting point. The "min" in His words "min ghammin" (from distress) may be for specifying the kind, and it may also be for the starting point, and it is a substitute for the first. The words "and taste" here contain an ellipsis; its estimated meaning is: and it will be said to them, "Taste." "Al-harid" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of muhrik, meaning burning.

The majority read "hadhani" with a light nun. Ibn Kathir alone read "hadhanni" with a heavy nun. Shibl also read it this way. It is a dialect of some Arabs with demonstratives, like alladhani and hadhani. Abu 'Ali mentioned this.

The majority read "hadhani" with a light nun. Ibn Kathir alone read "hadhanni" with a heavy nun. Shibl also read it this way. It is a dialect of some Arabs with demonstratives, like alladhani and hadhani. Abu 'Ali mentioned this.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verses 18–22:

The words of the Most High:

﴿Do you not see that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the creatures, and many of mankind; and many deserve the punishment. Whoever Allah disgraces, none can honor him. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.﴾

﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads, by which what is in their bellies and their skins will be melted.﴾ ﴿And for them are hooked rods of iron.﴾ ﴿Every time they want to get out of it from distress, they will be returned into it, and [it will be said], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾

"Do you not see" is an alert, from the sight of the heart. This verse informs that all created beings submit and are subservient to Allah the Exalted. The verse mentions everything that people worship, since among created beings there are greater things than those mentioned, such as the seas, the winds and the air. So "whoever is in the heavens" refers to the angels, and "whoever is on the earth" refers to humans who worship. "The sun" was worshipped by Himyar, who were the people of Bilqis. "The moon" was worshipped by Kinanah, as Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said. Tamim worshipped al-Dabaran, Lakhm worshipped Jupiter (al-Mushtari), Tayy worshipped al-Thurayya, Quraysh worshipped al-Shi'ra, Asad worshipped 'Utarid, and Rabi'ah worshipped al-Mirzam. "The mountains and the trees" include fire, idols of stone and wood. "The creatures" include cattle and other animals worshipped, such as the rooster and the like.

"Prostration" (al-sujud) in this verse means submission and compliance with the command. This is like the words of the poet:

"... you see the sand-hills in it prostrating to the hooves."

This is a case where ordinary prostration is impossible. Mujahid said: the prostration of these things is their being nullified. Some said: their prostration is the manifestation of craftsmanship in them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is an error; they confused this verse with the verse of glorification (tasbih). There, it is possible to say that it means the traces of craftsmanship.

The words of Allah, "and many deserve the punishment," may be coordinated with what preceded, meaning: and many deserve the punishment, prostrating unwillingly, that is, out of aversion and against their will, either by submitting when faced with hardships and the like. Mujahid said this, and said: their prostration is by their shadow. It may also be a nominative beginning (mubtada') cut off from what precedes it, as if the clause is set in parallel with the words "and many of mankind," because the meaning is that they are granted mercy through their prostration. This is supported by the words of Allah the Exalted after it: "Whoever Allah disgraces," and so on.

Most readers recited "fa-ma lahu min mukrim" with a kasra on the ra' (ra'). Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it with a fatha on the ra', meaning "from any place," or as a verbal noun (masdar) like madkhal. Most readers recited "wa-l-dawabb" with a doubled ba' (shaddah). Al-Zuhri alone read it with a single ba' (takhfif). This is rare and weak, and it is a lightening contrary to analogy, as they said: zallat and ahassat, and as 'Alqamah said:

"As if their ewer were a gazelle on a height, / Prepared with the threads of linen, veiled."

He meant: bi-sara'ib al-kattan (with the strands of linen). Abu 'Ali cited a similar example:

"Until, when I found nothing but evil, / I became a man of Malik ibn Ja'far."

This is a feature used only in poetry, so this reading is weak.

The words of Allah the Exalted: "These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord," and so on. People differed about what is indicated by "these two" (hadhani). Qays ibn 'Ubada and Hilal ibn Yasaf said: this verse was revealed concerning the duellists on the day of Badr. They were six: Hamzah, 'Ali, and 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, who came out against 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "I am the first to kneel down for the dispute before Allah on the Day of Resurrection." Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) swore to this statement.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It occurs that the verse about them is in the Sahih of al-Bukhari (may Allah have mercy on him).

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: the indication is to the believers and the People of the Book, because a dispute occurred between them. The Jews said, "We are older in religion than you," and similar things, so the verse was revealed. 'Ikrimah said: the dispute is between Paradise and Hell. Mujahid, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, 'Asim, and al-Kalbi said: the indication is to believers and disbelievers in general.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is a view that the verse supports, because the words "and many of mankind" came before, meaning: they are believers who prostrate. Then He said: "and many deserve the punishment," then He indicated these two categories with the words "these two adversaries." The meaning is that faith and its people, and disbelief and its people, are two adversaries, who have been in enmity, dispute and war since the beginning until the Hour arrives. The words "two adversaries" mean two groups, because the word khasm is a verbal noun that is used as an adjective for both the plural and the singular. What shows that He meant the plural is the words "they disputed" (ikhtasamu), which is the reading of most readers. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "ikhtasama" (dual). The words "concerning their Lord" mean: concerning the matter of their Lord, His attributes and His oneness. It may also mean: concerning the pleasure of their Lord, and concerning His essence.

Then He explained the ruling for the two groups. The Blessed and Exalted threatened the disbelievers with the punishment of Hell. "Qutti'at" means: garments were made for them by measure, as a garment is cut out. It is narrated that they are made of brass. It was said: there is no stone hotter than it when it is heated. It is narrated concerning the pouring of the hamim (boiling water) that their heads are struck with the hooked rods so that their brains are exposed, and then the hamim is poured. It was said: rather, the hamim is poured first, which does what is described, and then they are struck with the hooked rods after that. "Al-hamim" is boiling water. "Yusharu" means: it is melted. It was said: it means: it is squeezed. This expression is troubling. It was said: it means: it is cooked. From this is the saying of the poet:

"... the sun melts it, but it does not melt."

As for those who say "it is squeezed," what it resembles is that the hamim descends into the belly, each time it is poured, and scrapes and strips it. Abu Hurayrah narrated something similar from the Prophet (ﷺ): "It strips it, reaches his feet with it, and melts it, then it returns as it was." The majority read "yusharu." A group read "yusahharu" with a fatha on the sad and a shaddah on the ha'. "Al-miq'amah" (with a kasra on the mim) is a rod of iron with which the one being struck is beaten.

The words of Allah the Exalted "they wish" (aradu): it is narrated concerning this that when the flame of the fire rises, it lifts them up until they reach the gates of the fire, and then they wish to exit, and they are struck with the hooked rods, and the angels of punishment (al-zabaniyah) push them back. The "min" in His words "minha" (from it) indicates the starting point. The "min" in His words "min ghammin" (from distress) may be for specifying the kind, and it may also be for the starting point, and it is a substitute for the first. The words "and taste" here contain an ellipsis; its estimated meaning is: and it will be said to them, "Taste." "Al-harid" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of muhrik, meaning burning.

The majority read "hadhani" with a light nun. Ibn Kathir alone read "hadhanni" with a heavy nun. Shibl also read it this way. It is a dialect of some Arabs with demonstratives, like alladhani and hadhani. Abu 'Ali mentioned this.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verses 23–25:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾ ﴿And they were guided to good speech, and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah and the Sacred Mosque, which We made for the people equally, [for] the resident therein and the visitor, and whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing – We will make him taste a painful punishment.﴾

This verse is a counterpart to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. The majority read "yuhallawna" (يُحَلَّوْنَ) with a fatha on the yā' and the lām, and with its lightening (تخفيف), it is said: ḥalā al-rajulu and ḥaliyati al-mar'atu, when she became one possessing ornaments (ḥilyy). It was also said: it is from their saying: "lam yaḥil fulānun bi-ṭā'il" (so-and-so did not gain anything by it). The "min" in His saying, Exalted is He: "min asāwira" (مِن أساوِرَ) is for specification of kind (li-bayān al-jins), and it is possible that it is for partitive (li-tab'īḍ). "Al-asāwir" is the plural of siwār and iswār with a kasra on the hamza. It was said: asāwir is the plural of aswira, and aswira is the plural of sawār. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read: "min aswiratin min dhahabin."

"Al-lu'lu'" is the gem (jawhar). It was said: its small ones; it was said: its large ones; and the more well-known view is that it is a name for the gem. Nafi' and 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read: "wa-lu'lu'an" (وَلُؤْلُؤًا) with the accusative, as a conjunction upon the position (mawḍi') of "al-asāwir," because the sense is: they will be adorned therein with bracelets. This is the reading of al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Salam, Ya'qub, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, 'Isa, and Ibn 'Umar. Abu al-Fath took its accusative as being governed by an implied verb. The rest of the seven read: "wa-lu'lu'un" (وَلُؤْلُؤٌ) with the genitive, as a conjunction either upon the wording of "al-asāwir," in which case "al-lu'lu'" is other than the bracelets, or upon "al-dhahab," because bracelets may also be made of gold and pearls strung together, one upon another. This reading is narrated from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Talha, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and the people of Makkah. In the "Imam" (ʿUthmānic codex) an alif is established after the waw, as related by al-Jahdari, while al-Asma'i said: there is no alif in it. Yahya narrated from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, the hamzation of the second waw but not the first, while al-Mu'alla ibn Mansur narrated from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, the opposite of that. Abu 'Ali said: their hamzation, their lightening, and hamzation of one of them without the other are all permissible. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read: "li'la'an" (لِئَلِئًا) with a kasra on both lāms.

Allah informed about them regarding the wearing of silk because it is among the most complete states of the Hereafter. It has been related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever wears silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The affairs of the Hereafter resemble the affairs of this world only in names alone; as for their attributes, they are entirely different.

"Good speech" (al-ṭayyib min al-qawl): the statement "there is no god but Allah" and what follows it of the remembrance of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, His glorification and His sanctification, and the rest of the speech of the people of Paradise of conversation and good discourse, for indeed no idle talk is heard therein. "The path of the Praiseworthy" is the way of Allah, Exalted is He, to which He called His servants. It is possible that by "al-Ḥamīd" he means the way itself, and so it is attributed to Him in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: "and the abode of the Hereafter" (wa-la-dāru al-ākhira).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar⦆ – the verse. His saying: "wa-yaṣuddūna" (وَيَصُدُّونَ) its estimate is: wa-hum yaṣuddūna (and they are barring), and with this the conjunction of the present tense upon the past is made good. A group said: the waw is extra, and "yaṣuddūna" is the predicate of "inna."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This corrupts the intended meaning. Rather, the predicate is omitted and implied at His saying: "wal-bād," its estimate being: they have lost or they have perished. "Yaṣuddūna" came in the present tense because it is a verb of continuity (fa'ala yudīmūnahu), as in the saying, Exalted is He: ﴿those who believe and whose hearts are assured﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28] and the like.

This verse was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyah when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was barred from the Sacred Mosque. This is because no barring of that gathering was known before it, except that it may be meant as barring individuals from the people, and that did occur at the beginning of the mission. A group said: by "the Sacred Mosque" they meant all of Makkah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is correct, but he intended by the mention the important matter that is meant thereby.

The majority of the people read: "sawā'un" (سَواءٌ) with a raf', and it is in the position of the inchoative (ibtida'), and "al-'ākif" is its predicate. It was said: the predicate is "sawā'un," placed first, and this is the view of Abu 'Ali, and the meaning is: the one We made for the people as a qibla or a place of worship. Hafs, from 'Asim, read: "sawā'an" (سَواءً) with a fatha, and this is the reading of al-A'mash, and it admits two possibilities: one is that it is a second object of "ja'ala," and "al-'ākif" is raised by it, because it is a verbal noun in the sense of "equal," which is made to act as an active participle; the second possibility is that it is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from the pronoun in "ja'alnāhu." A group read: "sawā'an" with a fatha, and "al-'ākif" with a kasra, as a conjunction upon "al-nās." "Al-'ākif" is the one who resides in the town, and "al-bādī" is the one who comes to it from elsewhere. Ibn Kathir read in both connection and pause: "al-bādī" with a yā'; Abu 'Amr paused without a yā' and connected with a yā'; Nafi' read: "al-bādd" without a yā' in both connection and pause in the narration of al-Musayyabi, and Abu Bakr and Isma'il ibn Abi Uways; and Warsh narrated connection with a yā'. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read without a yā' in both connection and pause, and it is in the "Imam" without a yā'.

The people agreed on equality in the Sacred Mosque, and they differed concerning Makkah. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and a group with them held that the matter is likewise regarding the houses of Makkah, and that the one who comes has the right to alight wherever he finds, and the owner of the dwelling must shelter him, whether he wills or refuses. Sufyan al-Thawri and others said likewise, and so it was in the early period. Ibn Sabit said: their houses had no doors until thefts increased, so a man installed a door, and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, objected to him and said: Will you close a door in the face of a pilgrim to the House of Allah? He said: I only intended to protect their goods from theft. So he left it, and the people took to installing doors. A majority of the Ummah, among them Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: houses are not like the Mosque, and their occupants have the right to use them and to exclusively possess them, and on this is the practice today.

This difference is built upon the difference concerning Makkah: is it conquered by force (ʿanwatan), as is related from Malik and al-Awza'i, or by treaty (ṣulḥan), as is related from al-Shafi'i? Whoever holds it to be by treaty, equality in dwellings is far-fetched in his view. Whoever holds it to be by force may say: equality therein was determined by the imams who did not grant it to anyone as a fief, and the residence of whoever resides does so on his own account.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Did 'Aqil leave us any dwelling?" requires equality, and it is that they are owned yet prohibited, on both interpretations of his ﷺ saying: for it has been interpreted to mean that he inherited all the dwellings of Abu Talib and others, and it has been interpreted to mean that he sold the dwellings of the Banu Hashim when they migrated. Among the proof for the ownership of their houses by their occupants is that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, bought from Safwan ibn Umayya a house for the prison for four thousand. It is also valid that equality is at the time of the season, out of necessity and need, and the matter then goes outside consideration by force or by treaty.

His saying, Exalted is He: "bi-ilḥād" (بِإلْحادٍ). Abu 'Ubayda said: the "bā'" is extra, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"In a Yemeni valley whose upper part grows the shitt and whose lower part with the markh and the shabahan"

And from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Our spears guaranteed the provision of our dependents..."

And this is common. It is also permissible that the estimate is: and whoever intends therein people with deviation.

"Al-ilḥād" (الإلحاد) is inclination (al-mayl). This deviation and wrongdoing combines all sins, from disbelief down to minor sins. Because of the greatness of the sanctity of the place, Allah, Exalted is He, threatened for the mere intention of an evil deed therein, and whoever intends an evil deed and does not do it is not called to account for it except in Makkah. This is the saying of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and a group of the Companions and others. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: deviation in this verse is shirk. He also said, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: saying "No, by Allah" and "Yes, by Allah" in Makkah is deviation. Habib ibn Abi Thabit said: hoarding (ḥukra) in Makkah is deviation by wrongdoing.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The generality of the words encompasses all of this.

A group read: "wa-man yaridu" (وَمَن يَرِدُ) from al-wurūd (coming to), related by al-Farra'; but the first is clearer, more general, and more praiseworthy for the sacred place. This corrupts the intended meaning. Rather, the predicate is omitted and implied at His saying: "wal-bād," its estimate being: they have lost or they have perished. This is correct, but he intended by the mention the important matter that is meant thereby.

Whoever holds it to be by force may say: equality therein was determined by the imams who did not grant it to anyone as a fief, and the residence of whoever resides does so on his own account.

"In a Yemeni valley whose upper part grows the shitt and whose lower part with the markh and the shabahan"

And from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Our spears guaranteed the provision of our dependents..."

And this is common. It is also permissible that the estimate is: and whoever intends therein people with deviation.

This is the saying of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and a group of the Companions and others. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: deviation in this verse is shirk. He also said, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: saying "No, by Allah" and "Yes, by Allah" in Makkah is deviation. Habib ibn Abi Thabit said: hoarding (ḥukra) in Makkah is deviation by wrongdoing.

The generality of the words encompasses all of this.

﴿And [remember] when We settled Abraham in the place of the House, [saying]: Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circle it, those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate.﴾ ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from every deep mountain pass.﴾ ﴿That they may witness the benefits [meant] for them and mention the name of God over known days, over the livestock animals He has provided for them. So eat from them and feed the distressed poor.﴾

The meaning: Remember when We settled (baww'a). The form *baww'a* is the intensive (taḍʿīf) causative of *bā'a*, which means "to return." It is as if the one who settles someone returns him to a place. The word is also used in the sense of "to dwell," as in God's words: ﴿we settle in the Garden wherever we will﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. The poet said:

*How many a righteous companion of mine, I settled him with my own hands in the grave.*

Regarding the lām in His words "for Abraham" (Ibrahīm), one group said it is superfluous (zā'ida). Another group said that *baww'a* is treated as a verb that takes a complement with lām, like *ja'ala* (to make).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The more apparent view is that the first object of *baww'a* is omitted, its implied sense being "the people" or "the world." Then He said "for Abraham," meaning: this honour was for him, and the people were settled by his hands.

"The House" (al-bayt) is the Ka'ba. It is reported that God had made it a place of worship for Adam, peace be upon him. Then it was obliterated by the Flood and other things. When the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, came, God commanded him to build it. He came to its site and began seeking a trace. God sent a wind which uncovered for him the foundations of Adam, and he arranged its bases upon them.

His words, ﴿that you do not associate anything with Me﴾, address Abraham, peace be upon him, according to the view of the majority, as it has been related to us. The sense is: it was said to him, "that you do not associate anything with Me." 'Ikrima recited it as "that he does not associate with Me," in the third person, to convey the sense of the statement that was made to him. Abu Hatim said: In this recitation the kaf must be in the subjunctive, meaning: "lest he associate."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In the majority's recitation, the *an* may be explanatory (mufassira), and it may be a lightened form of the heavy *anna*.

The verse contains a reproach to those among the inhabitants of the House who associated others with God, meaning: this was the covenant with your father, and after him you, but you did not fulfil it; rather you associated others. A group said that the address in ﴿that you do not associate﴾ is to Muhammad ﷺ, and that he was commanded to purify the House and to proclaim the pilgrimage.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The majority hold that this was for Abraham, peace be upon him, and this is the more correct view.

The "purification of the House" is general, covering disbelief, innovations, all impurities, blood, and other things. "Those who stand" (al-qā'imūn) are those who pray. God mentioned the most important of the pillars of prayer, which are standing, bowing and prostration.

This was misread by Ibn Jinni, for he related from them *wa-adhina* (وَأذِنَ) as a past-tense verb, and he parsed it by making it a conjunction with *baww'anā*.

It is related that when Abraham, peace be upon him, was commanded to proclaim the pilgrimage, he said: "O Lord, if I call out, who will hear me?" It was said to him: "Call, O Abraham; upon you is the calling, and upon Us is the conveying." So he climbed Abu Qubays, and it is said, the Maqam stone, and called out: "O people, indeed God has commanded you to make pilgrimage to this House, so make pilgrimage." The reports differ on his wording, peace be upon him, but it must necessarily include mention of the House and the pilgrimage. It is related that on the day he called out, He made everyone who would perform pilgrimage until the Day of Resurrection, who were in the loins of men, hear him, and everything at that time, whether inanimate or otherwise, responded: "Here I am, O God, here I am." Those who adopted this distinction took "the mention of God's name" here to refer to slaughtering the sacrificial animals, the offerings, and so on. Reflect on this and its purpose will become clear to you. It appears that "known" and "counted" may have the same meaning, that is, all those virtuous days, and the matter of slaughter and of hastening is not tied to a counted or a known day. The purpose of His words "known" and "counted" is to encourage [devotion] on these days and to seize their virtue, since they are not like other days. It is as if He said: they are specially distinguished, so let them be seized.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿So eat﴾ is a recommendation. The scholars recommend that a man eat from his offering or sacrifice while giving away most of it in charity, though they permit giving all of it in charity and eating all of it. *Al-bā'is* (البائِسُ) is the one who has been touched by the harm of poverty and its misery. It is said: "the man became wretched" (ba'isa yab'us). It may also be used of one who has been struck by a calamity of time even if he is not poor. From this is his words, peace be upon him: "But the wretched one (al-bā'is) (p-241) is Sa'd ibn Khawla." The intended meaning in this verse is those in need.

Whoever associates others with God, it is as though he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind hurled him into a distant place.﴾

The recitation differed over the vowelling of the lam in His words ﴿Then let them (لْيَقْضُوا) ... and let them (وَلْيُوَفُّوا / وَلْيَطَّوَّفُوا)﴾: over reading all of them with a kasra, and over reading "liyaqdu" with a kasra while making the other two sukun. Included within this is the completion of all of the rites of Hajj, since the "tafath" is not finished except after these.

'Asim alone (in the transmission of Abu Bakr) read "wa-liyuwaffu" with a fatha on the waw and a shaddah on the fa'. "Wafa" and "awfa" are two dialects, both used in the Book of God, though "awfa" is more common. "Nudhur" (vows) refers to what they have with them of sacrificial animals and other things. "Tawaf" (circumambulation) mentioned in this verse is the tawaf al-ifadah (the circumambulation of return, which is one of the obligatory elements of Hajj). Al-Tabari said: there is no disagreement among the interpreters on this. Malik said: it is obligatory, and whoever abandons it must return from his homeland, unless he performs the tawaf al-wada' (farewell circumambulation), in which case it suffices for him.

The al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is possible, by the order of the sequence, that the reference is to the farewell circumambulation, since it is preferable that it be performed in any case. Al-Tabari transmitted with a chain from 'Amr ibn Abi Salamah, who said: I asked Zuhayr about His words ﴿and let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾, and he said: it is the farewell circumambulation.

Malik said in the Muwatta': The interpreters differed on the meaning of describing the House as "al-'Atiq." Mujahid and al-Hasan said: "al-'Atiq" means "the ancient," as one says "a sword that is 'atiq," and "'ataqa al-shay'" (it became old).

The al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is an opinion supported by reasoning, since it is the first house placed for mankind. However, Ibn al-Zubayr said: it was named "'Atiq" because God freed it from the tyrants by preventing them from it, and he narrated a hadith on this from the Prophet (ﷺ). But no reasoning stands against a hadith. Another group said: it was named "'Atiq" because it was never owned by anyone, and another group said: it was named "'Atiq" because God frees the necks of sinners from punishment within it.

The al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is refuted by morphology (al-tasrif). It was also said: it was named "'Atiq" because it was freed from the Flood, a view reported from Ibn Jubayr. It is possible that "al-'Atiq" is an adjective of praise implying the excellence of a thing, as 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said: "I rode a noble (ʿatiq) horse," in the hadith, and similar to this is their saying: "a free speech" (kalam hurr).

His words "dhalika" (that) may be in the nominative position, by the implied meaning: "your obligation is that," or "the obligatory thing is that." It may also be in the accusative position, by the implied meaning: "comply with that," and similar implied verbs. The best of implied things is the one whose explicit form is the best. Similar to this eloquent indication is the verse of Zuhayr:

"This (is so), and it is not like one who is incapable with his plan, amid the assembly, when one of the speakers speaks."

The "sacred rites" (al-hurumat) intended here are the actions of Hajj referred to in His words, glorified and exalted: ﴿Then let them end their untidiness and fulfil their vows﴾. Included in this is honouring the sacred sites, as Ibn Zayd and others said. He promised a reward for honouring them after this, as an encouragement and an incitement. Then the wording of the verse after this (ba'da dhalik) covers every sacred thing of God in the whole of the Law. His words "fahuwa khayr" (it is better) apparently do not mean comparative superiority, but rather a promise of good. It is possible to take "khayr" as comparative, by a figurative usage in this context.

His words ﴿And the cattle have been made lawful for you﴾ point to what the Arabs used to do by declaring things unlawful according to their own opinion, such as the bahirah and the sa'ibah. So God removed all of that and made all cattle lawful for them, except what is recited to them in the Book of God, blessed and exalted, in more than one place. Then He commanded them to shun the filth of idols. The statement allows two meanings. One is that "min" (in "min al-awthan," "of the idols") is explanatory of the genus, so the prohibition falls only on the filth of idols, and the rest of the filths are prohibited elsewhere. The second meaning is that "min" indicates the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah), as if He forbade them from filth in general and then specified for them its origin, from which it reaches them, since idol-worship gathers every corruption and filth. It also appears that the reference is to the sacrifices offered to idols, and so this would be among what is recited to them. Whoever says that "min" is partitive (lil-tab'id) has altered the meaning of the verse and corrupted it. The narration from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj is that the verse is a prohibition against worshipping idols.

Ibn Mas'ud and Ayman ibn Khuraym said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: the testimony of falsehood equals association (with God)," and he recited this verse. "Zur" is derived from "zawar," which means inclination, and from it comes the expression "fi janib fulan zawar" (there is deviation in so-and-so's side). It appears that the reference in the "zur" of their statements is to their declaring things unlawful and lawful concerning the cattle, which they had legislated.

"Hunafa'" (turning as true monotheists) means: upright, or inclining towards the truth, since the word "hanaf" is one of the words with opposite meanings, applying both to uprightness and to inclination. "Hunafa'" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Some said: "hunafa'" means pilgrims (hujjaj).

The al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a restriction for which there is no evidence.

"Ghayra mushrikin" (not associating) may be another circumstantial state, and it may be a qualifier of "hunafa'."

Then God struck a parable for the one who associates others with God, glorified and exalted, showing it at the extreme of falling. It may imply terror and the complete severance from salvation. This is unlike the parable He struck for the believer in His words: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in the false deities and believes in God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256]. Similar to this is the saying of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him: "If I narrate to you from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then to fall from the sky to the earth is easier for me than to lie against him," in the hadith.

Nafi' alone read: "fa-takhattafahu al-tayr" with a fatha on the kha' and a shaddah on the ta', by dropping the ta' of the tafa''ul form. The rest read: "fa-takhtifuhu al-tayr" with a sukun on the kha' and a lightened ta'. Al-Hasan, according to what is transmitted from him, read: "fa-tikhittafahu" with a kasra on the ta' and the kha' and a fatha on the shaddah'd ta'. Al-Hasan also, and Abu Raja', read with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the kha' and the ta' with a shaddah. Al-A'mash read: "min al-sama' takhtifuhu" without the fa', in a manner similar to the reading of the majority. He conjoined the present tense (al-mustaqbal) with the past tense (al-madi) because it is by implication: "so he is snatched by the birds." Abu Ja'far read: "al-riyah" (the winds) in place of "al-rih."

"Sahiq" means distant, and from it comes the expression "ashaqahu Allah" (God removed him far away). From it comes the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Then I will say: 'suhqan, suhqan'" (away, away), and from it comes "nakhlah suhuq," meaning a palm tree that is tall and far-reaching in the sky.

This is unlike the parable He struck for the believer in His words: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in the false deities and believes in God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256]. Similar to this is the saying of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him: "If I narrate to you from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then to fall from the sky to the earth is easier for me than to lie against him," in the hadith.

Nafi' alone read: "fa-takhattafahu al-tayr" with a fatha on the kha' and a shaddah on the ta', by dropping the ta' of the tafa''ul form. The rest read: "fa-takhtifuhu al-tayr" with a sukun on the kha' and a lightened ta'. Al-Hasan, according to what is transmitted from him, read: "fa-tikhittafahu" with a kasra on the ta' and the kha' and a fatha on the shaddah'd ta'. Al-Hasan also, and Abu Raja', read with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the kha' and the ta' with a shaddah. Al-A'mash read: "min al-sama' takhtifuhu" without the fa', in a manner similar to the reading of the majority. He conjoined the present tense (al-mustaqbal) with the past tense (al-madi) because it is by implication: "so he is snatched by the birds." Abu Ja'far read: "al-riyah" (the winds) in place of "al-rih."

"Sahiq" means distant, and from it comes the expression "ashaqahu Allah" (God removed him far away). From it comes the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Then I will say: 'suhqan, suhqan'" (away, away), and from it comes "nakhlah suhuq," meaning a palm tree that is tall and far-reaching in the sky.

(p-246)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verse 32–35:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿That, and whoever honours the rites of Allah, indeed it is from the piety of the hearts.﴾ ﴿For you therein are benefits until a specified term; then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House.﴾ ﴿And for every community We have appointed a rite, that they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided them of the livestock animals. So your God is one God, so submit to Him. And give good tidings to the humble,﴾ ﴿those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and the patient over what afflicts them, and those who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them.﴾

The estimated (implied) reading at this point is: the matter is that. "Sha'a'ir" (the rites, sing. sha'ira, i.e. everything dedicated to Allah the Exalted in which there is a command that makes it conspicuous and known). A group said: by the sha'a'ir in this verse is meant the sacrificial animals (al-hady) that are marked (al-mush'ira), and "honouring them" means fattening them, giving attention to their matter, and paying a high price for them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and a group. The pronoun in "fa-innaha" (indeed it) refers to the glorification and the act contained in the speech. "Al-qulub" (the hearts) has been read in the nominative, as the agent of the verbal noun which is "taqwa". Then the commentators differed concerning the Exalted's words: ﴿For you therein are benefits﴾ and so on. Mujahid and Qatada said: He meant that for people, in their livestock, there are benefits of wool, milk and other things, as long as its Lord has not sent it as a hady; when He sends it, that is "the specified term". 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: He meant: for you, in the hady that has been sent, there are benefits of riding and milking for whoever is compelled, and "the specified term" is its slaughter. "Thumma" (then) is for the ordering of sentences, because "the place of lawful release" (mahall) comes before "the term" (ajal). The meaning of the speech according to these two groups is: then its place of release is the place of sacrifice; the mention of the House is because it is the most noble of the sacred places and the intended destination of the hady and others. Ibn Zayd, Ibn 'Umar, and al-Hasan said: those rites in this verse are all the places of Hajj and its landmarks: Mina, 'Arafa, Muzdalifa, al-Safa and al-Marwa, the House and other things. In the verse that comes later, the camel is among the sha'a'ir. The "benefits" are trade and the seeking of provision, and it is possible that he meant earning reward and forgiveness; a group said both. The "term" is the return to Makkah and the Tawaf al-Ifadah (the circuit of overflowing).

The Exalted's words: "thumma mahalluha" (then its place of release) are derived from the release (ihlal) of the one in ihram, meaning: then He postponed all of this until the Tawaf al-Ifadah at the Ancient House. So the House, according to this interpretation, is intended in itself; this was said by Malik in (al-Muwatta').

Then the Exalted informed that He has appointed for every community among the nations a "mansak", that is, a place of worship and devotion. Then the mansak is a noun of place like "madhbah" (slaughterhouse) and the like, and it is possible that he meant by it the verbal noun, as if he said: worship and the like. "Al-nasik" is the worshipper. Mujahid said: it is the sunnah (established practice) in shedding the blood of sacrifices. Most of the reciters read "mansakan" with a fatha on the sin, and it is from "nasaka yansuku" with a damma on the sin in the imperfect. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "mansikan" with a kasra on the sin. Abu al-Fath said: the fatha is preferable, because it is either the verbal noun or the place, and both are with fatha; the kasra in this is among the anomalous forms in the noun of place, since (mafil) from "fa'ala yef'alu" like "masjid" from "sajada yasjudu", and analogy does not permit it there; and it seems that al-Kisa'i heard it from the Arabs.

The Exalted's words: ﴿that they may mention the name of Allah﴾ mean: We commanded them, at the time of their slaughtering, to mention Allah, and that the slaughter be for Him, because He is the provider of that. Then the wording turned from the report about the nations to informing those present with what means: so the God is one for all of you; likewise the matter in the sacrifice is only that it should be sincerely for Him. "Aslimu" (submit) means: for His right, His face, and His favour, believe and submit; it is possible that he meant surrender.

Then the Blessed and Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to give a glad tiding in absolute terms, and it is more eloquent than a specifying one, because it is unrestricted together with the utmost extent of imagination. "Al-mukhbitin" (the humble): the humble, submissive believers; "al-khabt" is what is low of the earth, and "al-mukhbit" is the humble one whose walk is subdued, as if he were on a descent of the earth. 'Amr ibn Aws said: "al-mukhbitun" are those who do not wrong, and when they are wronged they do not seek retribution.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a noble example of the character of the gentle, mild believer. Mujahid said: they are those who are reassured by the command of Allah the Exalted. He described them, the Exalted, as having fear and trembling at the mention of Allah, and that is due to the strength of their certainty and their observance of their Lord, as if they were before Him. He described them, the Blessed and Exalted, with patience, prayer, establishing prayer and maintaining it. The majority read "al-salati" with a kasra (as a genitive), while Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Hasan read "al-salata" with a fatha, as an accusative, supposing the nun and that its deletion is for lightening; it is narrated from Abu 'Amr. Al-A'mash read "wal-muqimina al-salata" with the nun and the accusative on "al-salata"; al-Dahhak read "wal-muqimu al-salata". It is narrated that this verse, the Exalted's words "wa-bashshiri al-mukhbitin" (and give glad tidings to the humble), was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all.
