**Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrat al-Ḥajj, verses 36–37**

[p. 249 marker in original]

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And the camels We have made for you as among the symbols of God. In them is good for you. So mention the name of God over them as they stand in ranks. Then when their sides fall (after slaughter), eat from them and feed the contented one and the beggar. Thus We have subjected them to you, that you may be grateful.﴾ ﴿Their flesh does not reach God, nor their blood, but piety from you reaches Him. Thus He has subjected them to you that you may glorify God for having guided you. And give good news to the doers of good.﴾

"Al-budn" (camels, the plural of "badanah") is the plural of "badanah," which refers to a camel or cow that has been marked (for sacrifice). It is said that it was so named because it "tabdunu," meaning it grows fat. It was also said that this name applies only to camels. A group said that "al-budn" is the plural of "badan," with a fatha on the *bāʾ* and *dāl*. Then they differed. Some of them said: "al-budn" is a singular noun of genus (*ism jins*) meaning a large, fat camel or cow. It is said of a fat man: "badun." Others said: "al-budn" is the plural of "badanah," like "thamarah" and "thumr." The majority read "wal-badan" with a sukūn on the *dāl*. Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah, al-Ḥasan, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read "al-budun" with a ḍammah on the *dāl*, and it may be the plural of "badanah" like "thumur." In this verse God enumerates His blessings upon people through these camels. The discussion of "al-shaʿāʾir" has already preceded.

As for "al-khayr" (good), it has been said about it what was said about "al-manāfiʿ" (benefits) which was mentioned earlier. The correct view is that it is general, encompassing the good of this world and the Hereafter. God's words "ʿalayhā" mean: at the time of slaughtering them (*ʿinda naḥrihā*).

The majority of people read "ṣawāff" with a fatha on the *fāʾ* and a shaddah, the plural of "ṣāffah," meaning obedient in their standing. Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Zayd ibn Aslam, Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, Shaqīq, Sulaymān al-Taymī, and al-Aʿraj read "ṣawāfī," the plural of "ṣāfiyah," meaning sincerely devoted to the Face of God, with no partner in them for anything, as the pre-Islamic people used to associate partners. Al-Ḥasan also read "ṣawāf" with a kasrah on the *fāʾ* and tanwīn, lightened, and it has the same meaning as the previous one, but the *yāʾ* was dropped for lightness, contrary to analogy (*ʿalā ghayr qiyās*). In this there is consideration (*naẓar*). Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī read "ṣawāfin" with a *nūn*, the plural of "ṣāfinah," which is the one that has raised one of its forelegs when tied, so that it does not tremble. "Al-ṣāfin" of horses is the one that raises one of its forelegs out of its excellence; it is also said one of its hind legs. From this is the words of God: ﴿the poised, well-bred steeds﴾ [Ṣād: 31]. ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm said:

*We left the horses clustered around it, their bridles hung, standing on three legs (ṣufūnā).*

"Wajabat" means: it fell after its slaughter. From it is "wajabat al-shams" (the sun set). From it is the verse of Aws ibn Ḥajar:

*Did not the sun and the full moon and the stars eclipse for the mountain that falls?*

God's words "fa-kulū" (then eat) are a recommendation (*nadb*). All scholars recommend that a person eat from his sacrificial animal. In this there is reward and compliance, since the people of the pre-Islamic period did not eat from their sacrificial animals. Mujāhid, Ibrāhīm, and al-Ṭabarī said: it is permission (*ibāḥah*).

"Al-qāniʿ" is the one who asks. It is said: "qanaʿa al-rajulu yaqnaʿu qanūʿan" when he asks, with a fatha on the *nūn* in the past tense. "Qaniʿa" with a kasrah on the *nūn* in the present, "yaqnaʿu qanāʿah," so he is "qaniʿ" if he refrains (from asking) and is content with his provision. This was said by al-Khalīl. From the first meaning is the verse of al-Shammākh:

*The wealth of a man, when it improves him, makes him rich from his needs; more chaste than begging.*

So the careful scholars said: "al-qāniʿ" is the one who asks.

"Al-muʿtarr" is the one who presents himself without asking. This was said by Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, Mujāhid, Ibrāhīm, al-Kalbī, and al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan. A group reversed this view. Al-Ṭabarī related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: "al-qāniʿ" is the one who is content with what you give him, and "al-muʿtarr" is the one who presents himself. It is also reported from him that he said: "al-qāniʿ" is the one who refrains (from asking), and "al-muʿtarr" is the beggar. It is reported from Mujāhid that he said: "al-qāniʿ" is the neighbor, even if he is rich. Abū Rajāʾ read "al-qāniʿa" (accusative). According to this interpretation, the meaning of the verse is: feed the one who is chaste, who does not come presenting himself. Abū al-Fatḥ ibn Jinnī held that he meant "al-qāniʿa" but dropped the *alif* for lightness.

This is far-fetched, because its interpretation as I mentioned just now is better, and this is resorted to only when no alternative is found. Abū Rajāʾ and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd read "al-muʿtarī," and the meaning is the same. It is narrated from Abū Rajāʾ (p. 251) "al-muʿtarr" with a lightened *rāʾ*. The poet said:

*By your life, the beggar does not come to our lands that we should prevent him with a wasted, oppressed one.*

Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him, held that the sacrifice is in thirds. Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad related from his father: "Feed the contented one and the beggar one third, the needy poor one third, and my family one third." Ibn al-Musayyib said: the owner of the sacrifice has only a quarter of it.

The author, Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

All of this is by way of preference (*istiḥsān*), not as obligation. Then God said: "Thus," meaning: just as I commanded you concerning them with all this, We subjected them to you. And "la-ʿallakum" (that you may) expresses hope on our part and in relation to our perspective.

God's words "yanāl" (reaches) is an expression of emphasis and affirmation, and it means: it will not rise in His estimation and attain a cause of reward. Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said: The people of the pre-Islamic period used to smear the House with blood, and the believers wanted to do the same, so God forbade that and this verse was revealed. The meaning is: rather, what reaches Him is elevation with Him, and the attainment of goodness in His sight is piety, that is sincerity and the performance of acts of obedience. Mālik ibn Dīnār, al-Aʿraj, Ibn Yaʿmar, and al-Zuhrī read "lan tanāla" and "wa-lakin tanāluhu" with a *tāʾ* in both.

The *tasmiyah* (saying the name of God) and *takbīr* (saying "Allahu akbar") over the sacrifice and the offering consists of the slaughterer saying: "In the name of God, and God is greatest." It is related that God's words "wa-bashshiri al-muḥsinīn" (and give good news to the doers of good) were revealed concerning the four Caliphs, may God be pleased with them all, as was mentioned in the preceding verse. But the apparent wording requires generality, covering every doer of good.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 22, verses 38–40:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed. Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate.﴾ ﴿Permission has been given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged, and indeed Allah is competent to give them victory.﴾ ﴿Those who were expelled from their homes without right, only because they say, "Our Lord is Allah." And were it not for Allah's repelling people, some by means of others, there would have been demolished monasteries, churches, prayer-places, and mosques in which the name of Allah is much mentioned. And Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Strong, Mighty.﴾

It has been related that this verse was revealed concerning the believers, when they had become numerous in Makkah and the disbelievers harmed them, and some of them migrated to the land of Abyssinia (al-Habasha). Some of the believers of Makkah wanted to kill whichever disbelievers they could reach, to assassinate, to betray and to deceive. So this verse was revealed, up to His saying "ingrate" (kafur). In it He promised defense, and He most eloquently forbade treachery and betrayal.

Nafi', al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far read *yudafi'u* (يُدافِعُ) and *wa-lawla difa'u* (وَلَوْلا دِفاعُ). Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read *yadfa'u* (يَدْفَعُ) and *wa-lawla daf'u* (وَلَوْلا دَفْعُ). 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *yudafi'u* and *wa-lawla daf'u*. Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: *Dafa'a* (دافَعَ) in this reading is treated like *dafa'a* (دَفَعَ), as in *'aqabtu al-liss* (I punished the thief) and *tara'aqtu al-na'l* (I repaired the sandal), so the verbal noun comes as *daf'an* (دَفْعًا). Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) and al-Akhfash said: Most of the speech is that Allah *yadfa'u*, and they say *dafa'a Allahu 'anka* (Allah repelled [harm] from you), except that *daf'* is more common.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

*Yudafi'u* is preferable in the verse, because there has arisen for the believers one who repels them and harms them, so his opposition and repelling of them is a *mudafa'a* (mutual defense) on their behalf. Al-Zahrawi related that *difa'an* (دِفاعًا) is the verbal noun of *dafa'a*, like *hasibtu hisaban* (I reckoned a reckoning). Then Allah, the Exalted, permitted the believers to fight those disbelievers who fought them, by His saying *udhina* (أُذِنَ, permission has been given). The form of the permission differs according to the readings, some being stronger than others. Nafi' and Hafs from 'Asim read *udhina* with a *damma* on the alif, *yuqatilun* (يُقاتِلُونَ) with a *fatha* on the ta', meaning "regarding their being fought," so the permission in this reading is clearly a recompense. Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read *udhina* with a *damma* on the alif, *yuqatilun* with a *kasra* on the ta', so the permission in this reading is at the beginning of fighting. Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *udhina* with a *fatha* on the alif, *yuqatilun* with a *kasra* on the ta'. Ibn 'Amir read both the alif and the ta' with a *fatha*. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: *udhina li-lladhina yuqatiluna fi sabil Allah* (with a *kasra* on the ta'). In the codex of Ubayy it reads *udhina* with a *damma* on the hamza, *li-lladhina qatalu* (for those who fought). Talha and al-A'mash read it likewise, except that they put a *fatha* on the hamza of *udhina*.

His saying ﴿because they were wronged﴾ means: the permission was granted on account of their having been wronged. Ibn Jurayj said: This verse was the first to abrogate the truce (al-muwada'a). Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: It was revealed at the migration of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Madinah. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: When I heard it, I knew that fighting would occur. Mujahid said: The verse concerns believers in Makkah who wanted to migrate to Madinah but were prevented.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What follows in the verse refutes this view, because those people were prevented from leaving, not expelled. Then the Exalted promised victory in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And indeed Allah is competent to give them victory.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who were expelled from their homes without right﴾ means every person whom Makkah rejected and whose people harmed him until they expelled him through their harm, some to Abyssinia and some to Madinah. He attributed the expulsion to the disbelievers because the discourse is in the context of establishing their sin and holding them accountable. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿only because they say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', اسْتِثْناءٌ مُنْقَطِعٌ), not part of the preceding clause. This is the view of Sibawayh, who does not permit a substitution (badal, بَدَل) here. Abu Ishaq permitted it, but the first view is more correct.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling people﴾ is a reinforcement of the command to fight. It mentions the wisdom of its benefit, and that this principle has existed among earlier nations. By it the laws were upheld and the acts of worship were gathered together. It is as if He said: Permission has been given for fighting, so let the believers fight. Were it not for fighting and jihad, the truth would have been overcome in every nation. This is the most correct interpretation of the verse. What has been said afterwards, such as defense, follows from jihad. Mujahid said: Were it not for Allah's repelling the wrong of one people by the testimony of just witnesses and the like. A group said: Were it not for Allah's repelling the oppression of oppressors by the justice of rulers. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Were it not for Allah's repelling, through the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), the disbelievers from the Successors (al-tabi'un) and those after them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this involves one people repelling another, but the meaning of fighting is more fitting to what preceded in the verse. A group said: Were it not for Allah's repelling punishment through the supplication of the virtuous and the righteous, and the like.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This and what resembles it corrupts the meaning of the verse, because the verse necessarily requires that there be people who are repelled and people from whom they are repelled. So consider this carefully.

Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read *lahudimat* (لَهُدِمَتْ) with a light *dal*. The rest read *lahuddimat* (لَهُدِّمَتْ) with a heavy *dal*.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The heavy form is preferable in that monasteries (sawami') are many, so their demolition involves repetition and multiplicity. As He, the Exalted, said: ﴿in towers well-built﴾ [al-Nisa': 78], where He made the *ya'* heavy, and He said "a lofty palace" (qasr mashid, قَصْرٍ مَشِيدٍ) [al-Hajj: 45], where He made it light because it is singular. From this also are ﴿and the doors were locked﴾ [Yusuf: 23] and ﴿with doors opened for them﴾ [Sad: 50].

*Al-sawma'a* (الصَّوْمَعَةُ) is the place of worship; its form is *fawla'a*. It is a tall, solitary building with a pointed top. *Al-sawma'* (الصَّوْمَعُ) among men means one with a hard heart. Before Islam, it was specific to the Christian monks and the worshippers of the Sabians, as Qatadah said. Then it was used for the minaret of the Muslims.

*Al-biya'* (الْبِيَعُ) are the churches of the Christians; its singular is *bay'a* (بَيْعَةٌ). Al-Tabari said: It is also said that they are the synagogues of the Jews.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Then he included, from Mujahid, what does not require that.

*Al-salawat* (الصَّلَواتُ) is shared by every religion. The word *hadm* (demolition) is borrowed for the prayers (salawat) from the point of view that they become inoperative; or he intended "places of prayers" (mawdi' salawat). A group held that *salawat* is a name for the synagogues of the Jews, and that the word is Hebrew, Arabicized, and not the plural of *salat*. Abu al-'Aliyah said: *Al-salawat* are the mosques of the Sabians. The readings of this word differ. The majority of people read *salawatun* (صَلَواتٌ) with a *fatha* on the *sad* and *lam*, and with a ta' marked by two dots below. This is either by the implied "places of prayers" (mawadi' salawat), or because the suspension of prayer is its demolition. Ja'far ibn Muhammad read *salwatun* (صَلْواتٌ) with a *fatha* on the *sad* and a *sukun* on the *lam*. A group read *silwatun* (صِلْواتٌ) with a *kasra* on the *sad* and a *sukun* on the *lam*, as recounted by Ibn Jinni. Al-Jahdari, as reported from him, read *wa-suluwatun* (وَصُلُواتٌ) with two dots above the ta' and a *damma* on the *sad* and *lam*, on the pattern *fu'ul*. He said: These are the mosques of the Christians. Al-Jahdari and al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf read *wa-sulubun* (وَصُلُوبٌ) with a *damma* on the *sad* and *lam* and a *ba'*, as the plural of *salib* (cross). Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi read *wa-sulutun* (وَصُلُوثٌ) with a *damma* on the *sad* and *lam* and a *tha'* marked with three dots. They said: These are the mosques of the Jews. A group read *salwatun* (صَلْوَتٌ) with a *fatha* on the *sad* and a *sukun* on the *lam*. A group read *wa-suluwatun* (وَصُلُواتٌ) with a *damma* on the *sad* and *lam*, as recounted by Ibn Jinni. A group read *sulawati* (صُلُوَتَيِ) with a *damma* on the *sad* and *lam* and a shortened alif after the ta', and Ibn Jinni related that outside the Gate of Mosul there are houses in which Christians are buried, called *salawat*. 'Ikrimah and Mujahid read *silwiti* (صِلْوِتَيْ) with a *kasra* on the *sad*, a *sukun* on the *lam*, a *kasra* on the waw, and a shortened alif after the ta'.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Khasif held that these names are intended to classify the places of worship of the nations: the *sawami'* are for the monks, the *bi'a* for the Christians, the *salawat* for the Jews, and the *masajid* for the Muslims. It has also been said: the *sawami'* are for the Sabians, the *bi'a* for the Christians, the *salawat* for the Jews, and the *masajid* for the Muslims.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The more apparent view is that the purpose is to emphasize the mention of the places of worship. The meanings of these names are found among the nations that have had a Scripture since ancient times. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verses 41–44:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil. And with Allah is the outcome of all affairs.﴾ ﴿And if they deny you, then the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud had denied [their messengers] before them,﴾ ﴿and the people of Abraham and the people of Lot,﴾ ﴿and the companions of Madyan. And Moses was denied, but I gave the disbelievers respite, then I seized them; so how was My rejection [of them]?﴾

A group said: this verse refers specifically to the four Rightly-Guided Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them.

(p-257) The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning of this specification is that these individuals in particular were empowered in the land from among those who fight, referred to at the beginning of the verse. The generality in all of this is clearer, and the command applies to all people. The verse is in fact a binding covenant upon everyone whom Allah Most High has empowered, each according to the measure of what he has been given. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verses 45–48:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿And how many a town did We destroy while it was doing wrong; so it lies in ruins upon its roofs, and [how many] a well abandoned and a lofty palace.﴾ ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth, so that they might have hearts with which to understand, or ears with which to hear? For indeed it is not the eyes that go blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind.﴾ ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will not fail His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.﴾ ﴿And how many a town did We give respite while it was doing wrong; then I seized it, and to Me is the final return.﴾

"Ka'ayyin" (how many) is the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) combined with "ayy", as stated by Sibawayh. I have already discussed at length the meaning of this word and its recitation in Surat Al 'Imran, in the verse: ﴿And how many a prophet﴾ [Al 'Imran: 146]. It is a word used for informing, and it may also come as an interrogative. Al-Farra' related: "Ka'ayyina ma laka?", meaning: "How much is what you have?" One group recited "ahlaknaha" (We destroyed it), and another group recited "ahlakat-ha" (it destroyed it) in the singular, and the intended meaning is the people of the town. "Zalima" means: by disbelief. "Khawiya" means: empty, and from it comes "khawa al-najm" when a star has become empty of its strength. Similar to it is "saqitatun 'ala 'urushiha" (fallen upon its roofs). "Al-'urush" means the roofs, so the meaning is that the roofs fell, then the walls collapsed upon them, so they are upon the roofs.

As for His saying: ﴿and a well abandoned﴾, it was said: it is coordinated with "al-'urush", and it was said: with "al-qarya" (the town), and this is more correct. One group recited "wa-bi'rin" with a hamza on the ya', which the majority softened. One group recited "mu'attalatun" with a fatha on the mim, a sukun on the 'ayn, a fatha on the ta', and without emphasis, while the majority read "mu'attalatin" with a damma on the mim, a fatha on the 'ayn, and a shadda on the ta'. "Al-mashid" means that which is built with plaster (al-shid), which is gypsum; and it was said: al-mashid is that which is raised high with baked brick or the like. From the usage of "mashid" is the verse of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

Shadahu marmaran wa-jallalahu kilsan, fa-li-l-tayri fi dhurahu wukur.
(He built it of marble and covered it with plaster; so in its heights are nests for birds.)

"Shadahu" means: he built it with plaster. The more apparent meaning in the verse is that he meant: he raised it with marble. One group said regarding this verse that "mashidan" means: raised high and fortified, and the sense of the verse requires that it was so before its ruin.

Then He rebuked them for heedlessness and abandoning reflection, by His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth﴾, that is, through the lands, so that they might look into the conditions of the nations that denied and were punished. This verse implies that intellect is in the heart, and that is the truth; nor does one deny that the brain has a connection with the heart, which causes the corruption of the intellect whenever the brain is disordered. His saying: "fa-takuna" is put in the accusative by the fa' in answer to the interrogative, the verb being shifted from the jussive to the subjunctive.

His saying: ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that go blind﴾ is an expression of emphasis, as if He said: blindness is not the blindness of the eyes; rather, true blindness is blindness of the heart. It is known that the eyes do go blind, but the intended meaning is what we have mentioned. This is like his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: "The strong man is not the one who wrestles well," and "The poor man is not this wanderer." The pronoun in "fa-innaha" refers to the matter (al-qissa) and what resembles it of the implied context. His saying: ﴿that are in the breasts﴾ is emphatic, like His saying: "with their mouths," and like when you say: "I looked at him with my own eye," and similar to this.

The pronoun in "wa-yasta'jilunaka" refers to the Quraysh. His saying: ﴿And Allah will not fail His promise﴾ is a threat and an information that everything is up to a determined time. The promise here is restricted to punishment, and therefore it occurs in the context of what is disliked.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years﴾: One group said: a day from the days of Allah's punishment is like a thousand years of what you count of these, because of the length and misery of the punishment; so the meaning is: how ignorant is one who seeks to hasten this. Another group said: a day with Allah, because of His encompassing it, His knowledge of it, and the execution of His power, is like a thousand years with you.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation implies that ten thousand years, and so on without end, are in the judgment of a thousand years; but they said: the thousand is mentioned because it is the final number without repetition, so it was limited to it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation does not suit the verse. Another group said: the meaning is that a day with Allah the Exalted is a thousand years of this reckoning. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I hope that my community will be delayed by half a day," and his saying: "The poor among the Muslims will enter Paradise before the rich by half a day, and that is five hundred years." And from this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: the measure of the reckoning on the Day of Resurrection is a thousand years. So the meaning is: even if the respite is long, it is within a portion of a day from the days of Allah.

He repeated His saying "wa-ka'ayyin" because it introduces another meaning: He first mentioned the towns that were destroyed without respite, but immediately after denial; then He added the one given respite, so that these [people] would not rejoice at the postponement of the punishment from them.

One group recited "ta'uddun" with a ta', and another group recited "ya'uddun" with a ya', as the third person.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verses 45–48:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿And how many a town did We destroy while it was doing wrong; so it lies in ruins upon its roofs, and [how many] a well abandoned and a lofty palace.﴾ ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth, so that they might have hearts with which to understand, or ears with which to hear? For indeed it is not the eyes that go blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind.﴾ ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will not fail His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.﴾ ﴿And how many a town did We give respite while it was doing wrong; then I seized it, and to Me is the final return.﴾

"Ka'ayyin" (how many) is the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) combined with "ayy", as stated by Sibawayh. I have already discussed at length the meaning of this word and its recitation in Surat Al 'Imran, in the verse: ﴿And how many a prophet﴾ [Al 'Imran: 146]. It is a word used for informing, and it may also come as an interrogative. Al-Farra' related: "Ka'ayyina ma laka?", meaning: "How much is what you have?" One group recited "ahlaknaha" (We destroyed it), and another group recited "ahlakat-ha" (it destroyed it) in the singular, and the intended meaning is the people of the town. "Zalima" means: by disbelief. "Khawiya" means: empty, and from it comes "khawa al-najm" when a star has become empty of its strength. Similar to it is "saqitatun 'ala 'urushiha" (fallen upon its roofs). "Al-'urush" means the roofs, so the meaning is that the roofs fell, then the walls collapsed upon them, so they are upon the roofs.

As for His saying: ﴿and a well abandoned﴾, it was said: it is coordinated with "al-'urush", and it was said: with "al-qarya" (the town), and this is more correct. One group recited "wa-bi'rin" with a hamza on the ya', which the majority softened. One group recited "mu'attalatun" with a fatha on the mim, a sukun on the 'ayn, a fatha on the ta', and without emphasis, while the majority read "mu'attalatin" with a damma on the mim, a fatha on the 'ayn, and a shadda on the ta'. "Al-mashid" means that which is built with plaster (al-shid), which is gypsum; and it was said: al-mashid is that which is raised high with baked brick or the like. From the usage of "mashid" is the verse of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

Shadahu marmaran wa-jallalahu kilsan, fa-li-l-tayri fi dhurahu wukur.
(He built it of marble and covered it with plaster; so in its heights are nests for birds.)

"Shadahu" means: he built it with plaster. The more apparent meaning in the verse is that he meant: he raised it with marble. One group said regarding this verse that "mashidan" means: raised high and fortified, and the sense of the verse requires that it was so before its ruin.

Then He rebuked them for heedlessness and abandoning reflection, by His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth﴾, that is, through the lands, so that they might look into the conditions of the nations that denied and were punished. This verse implies that intellect is in the heart, and that is the truth; nor does one deny that the brain has a connection with the heart, which causes the corruption of the intellect whenever the brain is disordered. His saying: "fa-takuna" is put in the accusative by the fa' in answer to the interrogative, the verb being shifted from the jussive to the subjunctive.

His saying: ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that go blind﴾ is an expression of emphasis, as if He said: blindness is not the blindness of the eyes; rather, true blindness is blindness of the heart. It is known that the eyes do go blind, but the intended meaning is what we have mentioned. This is like his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: "The strong man is not the one who wrestles well," and "The poor man is not this wanderer." The pronoun in "fa-innaha" refers to the matter (al-qissa) and what resembles it of the implied context. His saying: ﴿that are in the breasts﴾ is emphatic, like His saying: "with their mouths," and like when you say: "I looked at him with my own eye," and similar to this.

The pronoun in "wa-yasta'jilunaka" refers to the Quraysh. His saying: ﴿And Allah will not fail His promise﴾ is a threat and an information that everything is up to a determined time. The promise here is restricted to punishment, and therefore it occurs in the context of what is disliked.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years﴾: One group said: a day from the days of Allah's punishment is like a thousand years of what you count of these, because of the length and misery of the punishment; so the meaning is: how ignorant is one who seeks to hasten this. Another group said: a day with Allah, because of His encompassing it, His knowledge of it, and the execution of His power, is like a thousand years with you.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation implies that ten thousand years, and so on without end, are in the judgment of a thousand years; but they said: the thousand is mentioned because it is the final number without repetition, so it was limited to it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation does not suit the verse. Another group said: the meaning is that a day with Allah the Exalted is a thousand years of this reckoning. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I hope that my community will be delayed by half a day," and his saying: "The poor among the Muslims will enter Paradise before the rich by half a day, and that is five hundred years." And from this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: the measure of the reckoning on the Day of Resurrection is a thousand years. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah al-Hajj (22), verses 49–54:**

The Most High said:

﴿Say: O mankind, I am only a clear warner to you.﴾ ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a generous provision.﴾ ﴿But those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish. But God abrogates what Satan casts, then God makes His verses firm, and God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿That He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease and whose hearts are hardened. Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension.﴾ ﴿And that those who have been given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, so they believe in it and their hearts humbly submit to it. Indeed, God is the Guide of those who believe to a straight path.﴾

The meaning: Say, O Muhammad, "I am only a warner of the punishment of God. It is not up to me to hasten the punishment or to delay it beyond its time." Then He divided the state of the believers and the disbelievers: the believers will have the covering of their sins and His provision for them in Paradise. The word "al-Karim" (the Generous) here is an attribute of negation of blemishes, as you say, "a noble garment" (thawb karim). And the disbelievers who strive against the signs will have the punishment of the Blazing Fire. All of this is what He commanded him to say, that is: this is the meaning of my message, not what you wish for.

As for His saying, "sa'aw" (they strove), its meaning is: they devised and schemed, from al-si'aya (striving/running about). "Al-ayat" (the signs) are the verses of the Qur'an, that is: they schemed through denial and their other sayings. A group read "mu'ajizin" (seeking to frustrate), meaning "mughalibin" (seeking to overpower), as though they sought to make the bearer of the signs incapable, and the signs require their incapacitating, so it took the form of mufa'ala (reciprocal form). Some people interpreted "mu'ajizin" as thinking that they could overcome God the Most High.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is an interpretation outside the wording. A group read "mu'ajjizin" without an alif and with a shadda on the jim, meaning: making people incapable of faith, that is, causing them, through discouragement, to be incapable of faith. Abu 'Ali said: "mu'ajjizin" means: attributing to the Companions of the Prophet, may God be pleased with them, incapacity, as you say, "I declared so-and-so a sinner (fassaqtu) and accused him of adultery (zannaytuhu)," that is, I attributed that to him.

As for His saying: ﴿We did not send before you﴾ the verse is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the incident in which Satan cast into the Prophet's (ﷺ) wish.

"Tamanna" (to wish) in its well-known meaning is: to desire and to love. A group said that it has this meaning in the verse, and the intended meaning is that Satan cast his words because of what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had wished of closeness to his people and their following him. They said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wished for something that God, Blessed and Exalted, had not decreed, Satan found the way. So when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited "al-Najm" (Surah 53) in the mosque of Makkah, with the Muslims and the polytheists present, he reached His saying: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ [53:19] ﴿and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [53:20], Satan cast: "Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is to be hoped for." The disbelievers said: "This is Muhammad mentioning our gods in the way we wish," and they rejoiced at that. When he reached the prostration, all the people prostrated except Umayya ibn Khalaf, who took a handful of dust, raised it to his forehead, and said: "This is enough for me." [Al-Bukhari said: it was Umayya ibn Khalaf.] Some people said: it was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira; some said: it was Abu Uhayha Sa'id ibn al-'As. Then word reached the emigrants to Abyssinia that the people of Makkah had followed Muhammad (ﷺ), so they rejoiced at that. Some of them came and found that Satan's casting had been abrogated (nusikhat), and that the people of Makkah had been put to trial.

A group said: "Tamanna" means: he recited, and "al-umniyya" means: recitation. From this is the statement of the poet:

*He recited the Book of God on the first night and its last, and met the death-stroke of the fates.*

And from it is the statement of another:

*…………… *** he recited the Psalms of David at a leisurely pace.*

They interpreted His saying, "illa amani" (except wishes) as meaning: except recitations. This group said, regarding the cause of Satan's casting into the Prophet's (ﷺ) recitation, what was mentioned just before about the mention of the gods.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This narration in which there is "hunna al-gharaniqa" (they are the cranes) has occurred in the books of tafsir (exegetical works) and the like, but al-Bukhari did not include it, nor Muslim, and to my knowledge no well-known compiler has recorded it. Rather, the school of the ahl al-hadith (the scholars of hadith) implies that Satan cast, without specifying this cause or any other. There is no disagreement that Satan's casting was only of audible words by which the trial occurred. Then people differed about the form of this casting. What is in the tafsir works, and is the well-known view, is that the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke those words, and that Satan deceived him and whispered into his heart until those words came out on his tongue. It was narrated that Jibril (peace be upon him) came down to him after that and reviewed with him Surah al-Najm, and when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited it, Jibril said to him: "I did not bring you this." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Have I fabricated against God and said what He did not say to me?" He began to lament and grieve, and then this verse was revealed: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger…﴾ [22:52].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

My father, may God have mercy on him, told me that he met, in the East, some of the scholars and speakers who said: "This is not permissible for the Prophet (ﷺ), who is protected (ma'sum) in conveying the message. Rather, the matter is that Satan uttered a word which he made the disbelievers hear at the point when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ [53:19] ﴿and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [53:20]. And he brought his voice close to the voice of the Prophet (ﷺ), until the matter became confused for the polytheists, and they said: 'Muhammad recited it.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

And "tamanna" according to this interpretation means "talā" (recited), without doubt. This interpretation has been reported from the Imam Abu al-Ma'ali, may God have mercy on him, and others.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The messenger (rasul) is more specific than the prophet (nabi), and many prophets were not sent as messengers, and every messenger is a prophet. The "naskh" (removal) in this verse means: causing to depart, as you say, "the sun abrogated (nasakhat) the shade," and it does not mean lifting a ruling that had been established.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Al-Tabari went at length and fully expounded the chain of transmission (isnad) to establish that Satan's casting was upon the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ). The narrations differed in the wording. In some of them: "Those are the gharaqa"; in some: "Those are the gharaniq"; in some: "and indeed their intercession"; in some: "and indeed their intercession [feminine]"; and in some: "from them, intercession is to be hoped for."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

"Al-gharaniq" are the great nobles of high standing. From it is the statement of the poet:

*Welcome, O hunter of the gharaniq.*

His saying, the Most High: ﴿That He may make what Satan casts﴾ the verse. The lam in His saying "li-yaj'ala" (that He may make) is connected to His saying ﴿then God abrogates﴾. "Al-fitna" (the trial) is testing and examination. "Those in whose hearts is a disease" are the common disbelievers, and "those whose hearts are hardened" are among them the elite stubborn ones, such as Abu Jahl, al-Nadr, and 'Uqba. "Al-shiqaq" (dissension) is distance from good and misguidance, and being in a side other than the side of righteousness. "Ba'id" (far) means that it has reached them and gone deep; so their return from it is not hoped for.

Those "who have been given knowledge" are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). The pronoun in "annahu" (that it) refers to the Qur'an. "Fa-tukhbita" means: they become humble and submissive, and it is derived from "al-khabt," which is the low-lying land. A group read "la-hadin" without a yā' after the dal; a group read "la-hadi" with a yā'; and a group read "la-hadin" with tanwin and without the idafa. This verse is a counterpart to His earlier saying: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension.﴾

So when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited "al-Najm" (Surah 53) in the mosque of Makkah, with the Muslims and the polytheists present, he reached His saying: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ [53:19] ﴿and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [53:20], Satan cast: "Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is to be hoped for." The disbelievers said: "This is Muhammad mentioning our gods in the way we wish," and they rejoiced at that. When he reached the prostration, all the people prostrated except Umayya ibn Khalaf, who took a handful of dust, raised it to his forehead, and said: "This is enough for me." [Al-Bukhari said: it was Umayya ibn Khalaf.] Some people said: it was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira; some said: it was Abu Uhayha Sa'id ibn al-'As. Then word reached the emigrants to Abyssinia that the people of Makkah had followed Muhammad (ﷺ), so they rejoiced at that. Some of them came and found that Satan's casting had been abrogated (nusikhat), and that the people of Makkah had been put to trial.

A group said: "Tamanna" means: he recited, and "al-umniyya" means: recitation. From this is the statement of the poet:

*He recited the Book of God on the first night and its last, and met the death-stroke of the fates.*

And from it is the statement of another:

*…………… *** he recited the Psalms of David at a leisurely pace.*

They interpreted His saying, "illa amani" (except wishes) as meaning: except recitations. This group said, regarding the cause of Satan's casting into the Prophet's (ﷺ) recitation, what was mentioned just before about the mention of the gods.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This narration in which there is "hunna al-gharaniqa" (they are the cranes) has occurred in the books of tafsir (exegetical works) and the like, but al-Bukhari did not include it, nor Muslim, and to my knowledge no well-known compiler has recorded it. Rather, the school of the ahl al-hadith (the scholars of hadith) implies that Satan cast, without specifying this cause or any other. There is no disagreement that Satan's casting was only of audible words by which the trial occurred. Then people differed about the form of this casting. What is in the tafsir works, and is the well-known view, is that the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke those words, and that Satan deceived him and whispered into his heart until those words came out on his tongue. It was narrated that Jibril (peace be upon him) came down to him after that and reviewed with him Surah al-Najm, and when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited it, Jibril said to him: "I did not bring you this." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Have I fabricated against God and said what He did not say to me?" He began to lament and grieve, and then this verse was revealed: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger…﴾ [22:52].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

My father, may God have mercy on him, told me that he met, in the East, some of the scholars and speakers who said: "This is not permissible for the Prophet (ﷺ), who is protected (ma'sum) in conveying the message. Rather, the matter is that Satan uttered a word which he made the disbelievers hear at the point when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ [53:19] ﴿and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [53:20]. And he brought his voice close to the voice of the Prophet (ﷺ), until the matter became confused for the polytheists, and they said: 'Muhammad recited it.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

And "tamanna" according to this interpretation means "talā" (recited), without doubt. This interpretation has been reported from the Imam Abu al-Ma'ali, may God have mercy on him, and others.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The messenger (rasul) is more specific than the prophet (nabi), and many prophets were not sent as messengers, and every messenger is a prophet. The "naskh" (removal) in this verse means: causing to depart, as you say, "the sun abrogated (nasakhat) the shade," and it does not mean lifting a ruling that had been established.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Al-Tabari went at length and fully expounded the chain of transmission (isnad) to establish that Satan's casting was upon the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ). The narrations differed in the wording. In some of them: "Those are the gharaqa"; in some: "Those are the gharaniq"; in some: "and indeed their intercession"; in some: "and indeed their intercession [feminine]"; and in some: "from them, intercession is to be hoped for."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

"Al-gharaniq" are the great nobles of high standing. From it is the statement of the poet:

*Welcome, O hunter of the gharaniq.*

His saying, the Most High: ﴿That He may make what Satan casts﴾ the verse. The lam in His saying "li-yaj'ala" (that He may make) is connected to His saying ﴿then God abrogates﴾. "Al-fitna" (the trial) is testing and examination. "Those in whose hearts is a disease" are the common disbelievers, and "those whose hearts are hardened" are among them the elite stubborn ones, such as Abu Jahl, al-Nadr, and 'Uqba. "Al-shiqaq" (dissension) is distance from good and misguidance, and being in a side other than the side of righteousness. "Ba'id" (far) means that it has reached them and gone deep; so their return from it is not hoped for.

Those "who have been given knowledge" are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). The pronoun in "annahu" (that it) refers to the Qur'an. "Fa-tukhbita" means: they become humble and submissive, and it is derived from "al-khabt," which is the low-lying land. A group read "la-hadin" without a yā' after the dal; a group read "la-hadi" with a yā'; and a group read "la-hadin" with tanwin and without the idafa. This verse is a counterpart to His earlier saying: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension.﴾

(p-266)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verses 55–62:

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them suddenly or there comes to them the punishment of a barren day.﴾ ﴿The dominion on that Day belongs to Allah; He will judge between them. So those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, for them will be a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿And those who emigrated for the cause of Allah and then were killed or died, Allah will surely provide for them a good provision. Indeed, Allah is the best of providers.﴾ ﴿He will surely admit them to an entrance with which they will be pleased. And indeed, Allah is Knowing and Forbearing.﴾ ﴿That is so. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with and then is oppressed, Allah will surely support him. Indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾ ﴿That is because Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and because Allah is Hearing and Seeing.﴾ ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke other than Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Most High, the Grand.﴾

"Al-mirya" (doubt, suspicion) means "al-shakk" (doubt). The pronoun in His saying, "minhu" (about it), has the following views: one group said it refers to the Qur'an; another group said it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ); another group said it refers to what Satan had cast (into the recitation). Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said it refers to the prostration of the Prophet (ﷺ) in Surat al-Najm.

As for "al-sa'a" (the Hour), one group said it means the Day of Resurrection, and "al-yawm al-'aqim" (the barren day) is the Day of Badr. Another group said "al-sa'a" is the hour of their death or their being killed in this world, as on the Day of Badr or similar, and "al-yawm al-'aqim" is the Day of Resurrection.

The shaykh, the judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These two views are sound, because they preserve the division expressed by "aw" (or). Whoever makes "al-sa'a" and "al-yawm al-'aqim" both refer to the Day of Resurrection has spoiled the rank of "aw". The Day of Resurrection, or the day of total destruction, is called "'aqim" (barren) because no night comes after it and no day. The days are like outcomes, one following another, so it is as if the last day has become barren. This is a metaphor (isti'ara), and the whole of this verse is a threat.

As for His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿The dominion on that Day belongs to Allah﴾, what is apparent from it is that it refers to the Day of Resurrection, in which there is no dominion for anyone. It is permissible to intend by it the Day of Badr or similar, in that Allah's decree alone takes effect, everything else becomes void, and His judgment is executed against whomever He wills to punish. As for whoever interprets it as the Day of Resurrection, His saying ﴿So those who believed﴾ up to His saying ﴿a humiliating punishment﴾ coheres for him. Whoever interprets it as the Day of Badr or similar makes His saying ﴿So those who believed﴾ a new beginning (ibtida'), an informative statement about their condition, which is built upon their condition on that barren day of faith and disbelief.

As for His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And those who emigrated for the cause of Allah﴾, the verse begins with another meaning. It was revealed when 'Uthman ibn Maz'un and Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Asad died in Madina. Some people said: "Those among the emigrants who were killed are better than those who died a natural death." So this verse was revealed, placing them equal in that Allah, blessed and exalted, provides for all of them a good provision. This does not necessarily mean they are equal in merit, and the apparent meaning of the Shari'a is that the one who was killed is more excellent. Some people said: "The one killed and the one who died in the cause of Allah are both martyrs, but the one killed has the distinction of what befell him for the sake of Allah, the Exalted." The "good provision" may be understood as the provision of the martyrs with their Lord in the barzakh (intermediate realm), and it may be understood as after the Day of Resurrection in Paradise.

One group read "mudkhalan" (an entrance) with a ḍamma on the mim from "dakhala" (to enter), so it is taken as governed by an implied verb, its estimated form being: "fa-yadkhulūna mudkhalan" (so they will enter an entrance). Another group read "mudkhalan" with a ḍamma on the mim from "adkhala" (to cause to enter).

Al-Tabari narrated through an isnad from Salman ibn 'Amir, who said: Fadala Burudas was an amir over quarters. He went out with the funerals of two men, one of whom had been killed and the other had died naturally. He saw the people inclining toward the funeral of the one who had been killed, so he said: "I see you, O people, inclining toward the one who was killed and preferring him. By Him in whose hand my soul is, I do not care from which of these two graves I shall be raised. Recite the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And those who emigrated for the cause of Allah, then were killed or died, Allah will surely provide for them a good provision﴾ up to ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Forbearing.﴾"

As for His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿That is so. And whoever retaliates﴾ up to His, may He be glorified, saying: ﴿He is the Most High, the Grand.﴾ The meaning is: the matter is that. Then He, may He be exalted, informed about whoever among the believers retaliates against an unbeliever who wronged him. He promised the one who was wronged that He would support him. He named the wrongdoing in this verse by the name of the punishment, just as punishment is often named by the name of the wrongdoing. All of this is a figurative usage (tajawwuz) and extension of meaning.

It was mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning a group of believers who were met by unbelievers in the sacred month. The believers refused to fight them, while the polytheists insisted on fighting. When they fought, the believers exerted themselves and Allah, the Exalted, gave them victory. Then this verse was revealed concerning them.

As for His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿That is because Allah causes the night to enter into the day﴾, its meaning: the victory of Allah, the Exalted, for His friends and for the one who was wronged, is because He is capable of great things, whose power cannot be matched. He concisely expressed this by pointing with "dhalika" (that) to the victory, and He expressed the power by its details. He mentioned from it an example that cannot be claimed for anyone other than Allah, the Exalted, and He made the shortening of the night and the lengthening of the day, and the reverse, to be "iylaj" (causing to enter) as a figurative usage and a comparison. His saying: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾ means approximately what we have mentioned. One group read "tad'una" (you invoke) with a "ta" above, and another group read "yad'una" (they invoke). The indication in "ma yad'una min dunihi" (what they invoke other than Him) is: one group said it refers to Satan, and another group said it refers to the idols. The generality here is good.

Indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾ ﴿That is because Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and because Allah is Hearing and Seeing.﴾ ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke other than Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Most High, the Grand.﴾

"Al-mirya" (doubt, suspicion) means "al-shakk" (doubt). The pronoun in His saying, "minhu" (about it), has the following views: one group said it refers to the Qur'an; another group said it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ); another group said it refers to what Satan had cast (into the recitation). Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said it refers to the prostration of the Prophet (ﷺ) in Surat al-Najm.

As for "al-sa'a" (the Hour), one group said it means the Day of Resurrection, and "al-yawm al-'aqim" (the barren day) is the Day of Badr. Another group said "al-sa'a" is the hour of their death or their being killed in this world, as on the Day of Badr or similar, and "al-yawm al-'aqim" is the Day of Resurrection.

The shaykh, the judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These two views are sound, because they preserve the division expressed by "aw" (or). Whoever makes "al-sa'a" and "al-yawm al-'aqim" both refer to the Day of Resurrection has spoiled the rank of "aw". The Day of Resurrection, or the day of total destruction, is called "'aqim" (barren) because no night comes after it and no day. The days are like outcomes, one following another, so it is as if the last day has become barren. This is a metaphor (isti'ara), and the whole of this verse is a threat.

As for His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿The dominion on that Day belongs to Allah﴾, what is apparent from it is that it refers to the Day of Resurrection, in which there is no dominion for anyone. It is permissible to intend by it the Day of Badr or similar, in that Allah's decree alone takes effect, everything else becomes void, and His judgment is executed against whomever He wills to punish. As for whoever interprets it as the Day of Resurrection, His saying ﴿So those who believed﴾ up to His saying ﴿a humiliating punishment﴾ coheres for him. Whoever interprets it as the Day of Badr or similar makes His saying ﴿So those who believed﴾ a new beginning (ibtida'), an informative statement about their condition, which is built upon their condition on that barren day of faith and disbelief.

As for His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And those who emigrated for the cause of Allah﴾, the verse begins with another meaning. It was revealed when 'Uthman ibn Maz'un and Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Asad died in Madina. Some people said: "Those among the emigrants who were killed are better than those who died a natural death." So this verse was revealed, placing them equal in that Allah, blessed and exalted, provides for all of them a good provision. This does not necessarily mean they are equal in merit, and the apparent meaning of the Shari'a is that the one who was killed is more excellent. Some people said: "The one killed and the one who died in the cause of Allah are both martyrs, but the one killed has the distinction of what befell him for the sake of Allah, the Exalted." The "good provision" may be understood as the provision of the martyrs with their Lord in the barzakh (intermediate realm), and it may be understood as after the Day of Resurrection in Paradise.

One group read "mudkhalan" (an entrance) with a ḍamma on the mim from "dakhala" (to enter), so it is taken as governed by an implied verb, its estimated form being: "fa-yadkhulūna mudkhalan" (so they will enter an entrance). Another group read "mudkhalan" with a ḍamma on the mim from "adkhala" (to cause to enter).

Al-Tabari narrated through an isnad from Salman ibn 'Amir, who said: Fadala Burudas was an amir over quarters. He went out with the funerals of two men, one of whom had been killed and the other had died naturally. He saw the people inclining toward the funeral of the one who had been killed, so he said: "I see you, O people, inclining toward the one who was killed and preferring him. By Him in whose hand my soul is, I do not care from which of these two graves I shall be raised. Recite the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And those who emigrated for the cause of Allah, then were killed or died, Allah will surely provide for them a good provision﴾ up to ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Forbearing.﴾"

As for His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿That is so. And whoever retaliates﴾ up to His, may He be glorified, saying: ﴿He is the Most High, the Grand.﴾ The meaning is: the matter is that. Then He, may He be exalted, informed about whoever among the believers retaliates against an unbeliever who wronged him. He promised the one who was wronged that He would support him. He named the wrongdoing in this verse by the name of the punishment, just as punishment is often named by the name of the wrongdoing. All of this is a figurative usage (tajawwuz) and extension of meaning.

It was mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning a group of believers who were met by unbelievers in the sacred month. The believers refused to fight them, while the polytheists insisted on fighting. When they fought, the believers exerted themselves and Allah, the Exalted, gave them victory. Then this verse was revealed concerning them.

As for His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿That is because Allah causes the night to enter into the day﴾, its meaning: the victory of Allah, the Exalted, for His friends and for the one who was wronged, is because He is capable of great things, whose power cannot be matched. He concisely expressed this by pointing with "dhalika" (that) to the victory, and He expressed the power by its details. He mentioned from it an example that cannot be claimed for anyone other than Allah, the Exalted, and He made the shortening of the night and the lengthening of the day, and the reverse, to be "iylaj" (causing to enter) as a figurative usage and a comparison. His saying: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾ means approximately what we have mentioned. One group read "tad'una" (you invoke) with a "ta" above, and another group read "yad'una" (they invoke). The indication in "ma yad'una min dunihi" (what they invoke other than Him) is: one group said it refers to Satan, and another group said it refers to the idols. The generality here is good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verse 63–65:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green? Indeed, Allah is Subtle, Aware.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you whatever is on the earth, and the ship that sails through the sea by His command, and that He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission? Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful to the people.﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: "Have you not seen" is an alert, and after it comes the report: that Allah sends down water from the sky, and the earth thereupon turns green. His saying "fa-tusbihu" (and so it becomes) is equivalent to His saying "fa-tudhhi" (and so it becomes bright) or "fa-tasir" (and so it becomes); it is an expression of the swiftness of its (the earth's) greening following the descent of the water and its continuance in that state customarily. The word "fa-tusbihu" is in the nominative because it is a predicate (khabar) in the position of the clause, and the fa is conjunctive (ʿatifa), not a response (jawab), because its being a response to His saying "Have you not seen" yields a corrupt meaning. It is related from ʿIkrima that he said: "This does not happen except in Mecca or Tihama."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The meaning of this is that he took His saying "fa-tusbihu" as intended for the morning after the night of rain, and held that this greening in the rest of the lands is delayed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

I have witnessed this in the Far Sus, where rain fell after a drought, and that sandy land which the winds had scattered became green with weak, fine vegetation. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "mukhdarratan" (green, feminine accusative), and a group read "mukhdarratun" (nominative). "Al-Latif" (the Subtle) means the one who arranges affairs with gentleness, and the lam in "lahu" (to Him) is the lam of possession; "al-Ghani" (the Free of need) is the one who has no need of anything, this is so in an absolute sense.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿He has subjected to you whatever is on the earth﴾ means: of animals, minerals and all other benefits. The majority read "wa-l-fulka" (and the ship) in the accusative, and this admits of two grammatical interpretations: first, that it is a conjunction upon "ma" (what), with the implied sense "and He subjected the ship"; second, that it is a conjunction upon the (understood) "anna" clause, with the implied sense "and that the ship". His saying "tajri" (sails) is, under the first grammatical reading, in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and under the second reading in the position of the predicate. A group read "wa-l-fulku" (and the ship) in the nominative, so "tajri" is the predicate under this reading.

His, the Exalted, saying: "except by His permission" may mean the Day of Resurrection, as if the folding of the sky and the loss of this configuration is like its falling. It may also mean a warning to them, that if He permits the sky to fall upon you, it will fall. It may also be that His saying "except by His permission" refers back to "holding back"; since the context implies "without pillars and the like," it is as if He meant: "except by His permission, so by Him do we hold it up." The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verses 66–69:

The Exalted's words:

﴿It is He who gave you life, then will cause you to die, then will give you life again. Indeed, mankind is ungrateful.﴾ ﴿For every community We have appointed rites (mansak) which they perform, so let them not dispute with you in the matter, and invite to your Lord. Indeed, you are upon a straight guidance.﴾ ﴿And if they argue with you, say: "Allah is most knowing of what you do."﴾ ﴿Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein you used to differ.﴾

The giving of life and causing of death in this verse are three stages, and the first death, which is explicitly mentioned in other places, has dropped out of it; yet it is implied in this verse. "Mansak" is a verbal noun (masdar), so it means worship and sacred law (shari'ah), and it is also a place of ritual sacrifice (nusuk). One group recited it with a fatha on the sin, and another with a kasra, and the discussion of this was already mentioned in this surah. The saying of the Exalted, "hum nasikuhu" (﴿they perform it﴿), indicates that "mansak" is the verbal noun; had it been the place, He would have said "hum nasikuna fihi" (they perform in it). A group reported that this verse was revealed due to the disputation of the disbelievers regarding the matter of slaughtered animals, and their saying to the believers: "Do you eat what you slaughter, while it is from your killing, and you do not eat what Allah has killed (of carrion)?" So the verse was revealed because of this dispute. The Exalted's words, ﴿so let them not dispute with you in the matter﴾, this clear form of the verb and prohibition may carry the meaning of intimidation, and may carry the meaning of belittling the doer and that he is less than that he should be contended with; and this is the meaning in this verse. Abu Ishaq said: the meaning is: "So do not dispute with them, lest they dispute with you."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This assumed interpretation that has been proposed is only appropriate with the meaning of intimidation, and it is only appropriate to assume here the meaning: "Do not begin with them by disputing with them." The prohibition is meant with a meaning beyond the wording, as is meant in their saying: "Let me not see you here" (la ara-nnaka hahuna), i.e., do not be here. One group recited: "fa-la yanza'nnaka" (so let them not draw you away). The Exalted's words, "fi al-amr" (in the matter), mean, according to the interpretation that "mansak" is the sacred laws: they do not dispute with you concerning the religion, the Book and the like; and according to the interpretation that "mansak" is the place of slaughter, as the aforementioned group reported, that the verse was revealed concerning slaughtered animals, then "al-amr" means the slaughter. And "al-huda" (guidance) in this verse means guidance and direction.

The Exalted's words, ﴿And if they argue with you﴾, the verse is a pure truce, abrogated by the verse of the sword; and the rest of the verse is a warning.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Do you not know that Allah knows whatever is in the heaven and the earth? Indeed, that is in a Book. Indeed, that for Allah is easy.﴾ ﴿And they worship besides Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and that of which they have no knowledge. And for the wrongdoers there will be no helper.﴾ ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them as clear evidences, you recognize in the faces of those who disbelieve the denial. They almost assault those who recite to them Our verses. Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that? The Fire, which Allah has promised to those who disbelieve, and wretched is the destination."﴾

When Allah, exalted is He, informed in the verse before it that He judges among the people on the Day of Resurrection concerning what they differed about, He followed that report with the statement that with Him is the knowledge of everything, so that the judgment falls upon something known. The expression thus came in the manner of an illustration of Allah's knowledge and His encompassing of everything, and that all of it is in a Book, which is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, that for Allah is easy﴾, the reference may be to the fact that this is in a Book and that it is known, and it may be a reference to the judgment concerning the disputes.

Then He mentioned, by way of rebuke, the act of the disbelievers in that they worship, besides Allah, idols for which Allah has sent down no proof or evidence. And "sultan" means proof wherever it occurs in the Noble Qur'an. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And for the wrongdoers there will be no helper﴾ is a threat.

The pronoun in "ʿalayhim" refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the meaning is that whenever they heard the Qur'an from the Prophet (ﷺ) or from one of his companions, and heard in it the rejection of their gods and the call to monotheism, the displeasure became apparent in their faces. The "munkar" is from their belief, their enmity, and that they plot and hasten to assault the one who recites. The meaning is that they almost assault them throughout their entire lifetime; but at rare times, the reciters were indeed assaulted, as happened to ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, and to the Prophet (ﷺ) when Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) came to his aid and resolved the matter, and to ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) when al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il gave him protection, and to Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him), and other than that. And "al-satw" is inflicting violence through physical assault or the command to do so.

Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to say to them, by way of threat and reproach: "Shall I inform you" — that is, "I inform you of something worse than that." The reference of "that" (dhalikum) is to the assault. Then he began to inform, as if someone had said to him, "And what is it?" He said: "The Fire," that is, the Fire of Jahannam. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿which Allah has promised to those who disbelieve﴾ may mean that Allah promised them the Fire, so the promise is of evil and the like, because of what is explicitly stated, and it did not come unrestricted. It may also mean that Allah, exalted is He, promised the Fire that it would be fed the disbelievers, so the promise is in its proper sense, which is required by its eagerness toward the disbelievers and its saying: ﴿Is there any more?﴾ [Qaf: 30] and the like of its evils. And "al-masir" is a noun of place from "sara," indicating a transition from one state to another.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The words of al-Tabari in this verse imply that the reference of "dhalikum" is to the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) who recite, then he said: "Shall I inform you of something more hateful to you than these: you are those who have been promised the Fire?" A saying similar to this has been attributed to an unnamed speaker, and all of this is weak.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verses 73–74:

His Exalted Majesty said:

﴿O mankind, a parable is presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it. And if the fly should snatch away from them something, they could not retrieve it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought.﴾ ﴿They have not appraised Allah with His true appraisal. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty.﴾

The address with His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿O mankind﴾: it has been said that it is an address encompassing the whole world. It has also been said that it is an address to the believers of that time, whom Allah, Exalted is He, intended to make clear to them the error of the disbelievers. There is no doubt that those addressed are these, but it is an address that encompasses all people: whenever anyone considers the matter of worshipping idols, the address is directed to him.

The interpreters (al-muta'awwilun) differed concerning the agent of "ḍuriba" (was presented): who is it? One group said: the meaning is that the people of disbelief presented their idols and images as a parable for Allah. So listen, you people, to the matter of these deities. Another group said: the meaning is that Allah, Exalted is He, presented a parable for these idols, which is such-and-such. So the example and the parable in the first interpretation are the idols, and the one for whom the example is made is Allah, Exalted is He; the example in the second interpretation is the fly and its affair, and that for which it is made is the idols. The meaning of "ḍuriba" is: was established and imposed. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Humiliation was imposed upon them﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 112], and our saying: "the poll-tax (jizya) was imposed" and "resurrection was established." It is also possible that "ḍuriba al-mathal" (a parable was presented) is from the striking (ḍarb) which is the parable, and from your saying: "this is the like (ḍarb) of this," as if he said: a likeness of a likeness.

One group read "yadʿūna" (you invoke) with a yāʾ at the beginning, the pronoun referring to the disbelievers. Another group read "yudʿawna" with a damma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the ʿayn, in the passive form whose agent is not named, the pronoun referring to the idols.

Allah, Exalted is He, began with the negation of creation and origination from them, since it is an established attribute proper to Him, as if He said: they have no share in My attribute. Then He followed it with the matter that reached the utmost of incapacity for them. He mentioned the snatching away by the fly because it was frequent and perceptible among the Arabs, for they used to perfume their idols with various kinds of perfume, and the fly would carry that off, and they were distressed by this aspect, so it was made a parable. "Dhubāb" (fly) has the plural "adhubba" in the few and "dhibbān" in the many, like ghurāb (crow): aghriba and ghirbān. And "dhubābāt" is not said except of the tails (of horses), not of animals.

The interpreters differed concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾. One group said: by the seeker He meant the idols, and by the sought the fly; that is, they ought to be seekers of what was taken from their perfume, according to the customary sense of honour in animals. Another group said: its meaning is that the disbelievers were weak in seeking from the idols the right course and virtue, and the idols were weak in giving that and granting it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that He intends: the seeker, who is the fly, is weak in snatching what is upon the idols, and the idols are weak in that they have no defence. In any case, the weakness of the fly, which is perceptible and agreed upon, indicates the weakness of the idols in having no defence against this, which is agreed upon as weak, and that the idols are in the lowest rank and most abject station.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They have not appraised Allah with His true appraisal﴾ is an address to the people mentioned, and the pronoun in "qadarū" refers to the disbelievers. The meaning: they did not render Him His due of glorification and monotheism. Then He informed of the might of Allah, Exalted is He, and His might, and these are two attributes contrary to the impotence of the idols.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 22, verses 75–77:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Allah chooses messengers from the angels and from mankind. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and to Allah all matters are returned.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, bow down, prostrate yourselves, worship your Lord, and do good, that you may succeed.﴾

It is narrated that this verse, up to His saying "al-umur" (matters), was revealed on account of the statement of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?﴾ [Sad: 8], and so Allah the Exalted informed that He "chooses" (yastafi), i.e., ﴿from the angels, messengers﴾ to the prophets and others, as reported in the hadiths, ﴿and from mankind﴾, who are the prophets sent to reform creation, those in whom prophethood (nubuwwah) and messengership (risalah) are combined.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿what is before them and what is behind them﴾ is an expression for the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of them. Its literal meaning is: the events before them and the events after them. "Al-umur" is the plural of "amr", and it is not intended to mean the verbal noun (masdar).

Then Allah the Exalted commanded His worship, and singled out bowing and prostration for mention, honouring the prayer (salah).

People differed as to whether there is a prostration (sajdah) in this verse. The position of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, is that he does not prostrate here. His saying the Exalted: ﴿and do good﴾ is a recommendation (nadb) regarding what is other than the obligatory duties whose obligation is established from other than this passage. His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿that you may succeed﴾ is an expression of hope (taraijji) with regard to the believers, like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿perhaps he may remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44]. And "al-falah" (success) in this verse is attaining the desired aim and reaching the hoped-for goal.
